I keep a list of what I'd do if Liscor were ever truly tested. It's a good list. It lives in the bottom drawer, and I hope it stays there.

speaker: Olesm
text: Back to the top.

speaker: Olesm
text: Stay bored, Olesm.

speaker: Olesm
text: So do I. You train your whole life for a day you pray never comes. Meanwhile the list stays in the drawer and I check the granary sums instead. Liscor's had ten quiet years. I like to think a few of them are partly mine.

speaker: Olesm
text: Anytime.

speaker: Olesm
text: A Raskghar, awake, under my streets. I get to write that sentence into the minutes now, and initial it. I'm filing this under 'problems the Council pays adventurers for' — which, as of today, includes you. The seal will hold. Probably. Play chess with me sometime; you've earned the good board.

speaker: Olesm
text: We should compare notes sometime.

speaker: Olesm
text: Back to the top.

speaker: Olesm
text: I've kept you long enough.

speaker: Olesm
text: The gap in the south wall? The masons watch that; it's on every list the Council owns. The one I lose sleep over is supply. Liscor has never been besieged long enough to learn its own granaries, and my arithmetic gives out in the third hungry week. You already knew that. I can see you did. It is, honestly, a relief not to be the only one in the room doing that arithmetic.

speaker: Olesm
text: Back to the top.

speaker: Olesm
text: Count on it.

speaker: Olesm
text: I would like that. Genuinely. Bring a board. One afternoon, the wall first, then the war — I'll have the supply figures out before you're through the door.

speaker: Olesm
text: [Charming Smile] You've been dreading that door since the survey. Sign it and sleep.

speaker: Olesm
text: Then I'll fund the first season myself, and you can explain the second. (12 gold)

speaker: Olesm
text: I'll come back when I've thought it through.

speaker: Olesm
text: Fed, on a schedule, with no end written anywhere. A posting like that sits on the ledger forever. Every quarter, somebody new asks why we're paying a Gnoll to walk down and feed a door, and every quarter somebody has to be brave enough to sign it again.

speaker: Olesm
text: Somebody has to hold the door.

speaker: Olesm
text: Get some sleep, Olesm.

speaker: Olesm

speaker: Olesm

text: My thanks.

speaker: Forge-Tier Clerk

text: I'll take the commission.

speaker: Forge-Tier Smith
text: That sounds like a fight between you and the examiner.

speaker: Forge-Tier Smith
text: I'll look at the hall.

speaker: Forge-Tier Smith

speaker: Forge-Tier Smith
text: Understood.

speaker: Forge-Tier Smith
text: It walks its own tolerance and corrects late. A slab picks up a scratch. A person picks up the kind of injury you spend a season paying off, so keep clear of the rig while it settles.

speaker: Forge-Tier Smith
text: [The standard measures recovery. It's printed on his own notice.]

speaker: Forge-Tier Smith
text: [Show her the billet you ran.]

text: [Tell her what happened to the calibration rig.]

text: [Tell her the argument is settled.]

text: Still working on it.

text: Well? Say it in the order it happened.

speaker: Forge-Tier Smith
text: She earned it.

speaker: Forge-Tier Smith
text: Then it is filed and it is finished. The bench is mine again until second bell.

speaker: Forge-Tier Smith
text: The rig is honest again and my apprentice gets a fair reading. Hand me the tongs — no, the short ones. She has forty-two on the board and I want the slab hot before second bell.

speaker: Forge-Tier Smith
text: You ran it once and it came back. She has run it forty-one times and it came back too. Now the file says so. Pull the vent chain on your way past. I have a billet in and she will want the bench.

speaker: Forge-Tier Smith
text: I have been arguing with that man for six years and it turns out we agreed all six years. It is in the file now. She will read it in the morning.

speaker: Forge-Tier Smith
text: What's the bench rated for?

speaker: Forge-Tier Smith
text: Who decides how a thing gets built up here?

speaker: Forge-Tier Smith
text: [Ask what the seal news cost the tier.]

speaker: Forge-Tier Smith
text: I'll let you work.

speaker: Forge-Tier Smith
text: Nine blades in your reject bin, all failed the same way.

speaker: Forge-Tier Smith
text: About your commission.

speaker: Forge-Tier Smith
text: Bench is mine until the second bell. Say it quick.

speaker: Forge-Tier Smith
text: You put the miscalibrated one down. It had been drifting toward my slab for two shifts. Say what you need.

speaker: Forge-Tier Smith
text: The Liscor news came up the shaft this morning. Say what you need while the billet heats.

speaker: Forge-Tier Smith
text: It was older than the city over it.

speaker: Forge-Tier Smith
text: That's most of it.

speaker: Forge-Tier Smith
text: Something under their stone wanted feeding, and now it doesn't. Nothing else reached this tier. I'd have liked the measurements.

speaker: Forge-Tier Smith
text: How often does someone push it?

speaker: Forge-Tier Smith
text: Then I'll stand clear of it.

speaker: Forge-Tier Smith
text: A full working day at heat, then it stands down cold. Push it past that and the slab cracks. A cracked slab is a season of paperwork before the city clears it again. The hammer hangs on its peg for all of it.

speaker: Forge-Tier Smith
text: Things fail loudly instead?

speaker: Forge-Tier Smith
text: Understood.

speaker: Forge-Tier Smith

speaker: Grimalkin
text: Understood.

speaker: Grimalkin
text: Grip, cleared. Wind, cleared — barely. The last measure was whether you quit before I did. You did not. The numbers say you will survive the forge tier. The file will say 'adequate.' Ask around this office what I usually write.

speaker: Grimalkin
text: What does that cost me?

speaker: Grimalkin
text: I'll take that reading another day.

speaker: Grimalkin
text: I have. The forge tier runs on rune-fed work. Every ward up there eats on a schedule a smith keeps in a ledger. Two feedings a shift, logged. No smith keeps one for your door. Stand still.

speaker: Grimalkin
text: Understood.

speaker: Grimalkin
text: It costs whatever it is drawing on, and it has been drawing unsupervised since long before you owned it. I do not find that alarming. I find it unmeasured. Find what sits at the far end of the draw and bring me the numbers. I will publish them and you will be a footnote.

speaker: Grimalkin
text: I'm here for the forge-tier fitness read. (8 gold)

speaker: Grimalkin
text: About the studies.

speaker: Grimalkin
text: Reporting in on the study.

speaker: Grimalkin
text: You've been about to say something since the stamp.

speaker: Grimalkin
text: Stand up straight when you address me. I measure everything that comes through this office, and most of it is found wanting. State your business.

speaker: Grimalkin
text: The field subject returns. Your engagement data survived review. It is in the literature now, fourth appendix, entered under a subject number. State your business.

speaker: Grimalkin
text: The casting subject. Your wind held past the eighth measure. The file has it already. Speak.

speaker: Grimalkin
text: The forge tier settled its temper argument and my name is in the file twice. The examiners log recovery on the blades now, same measure as a squat. Depth, then recovery, then it goes in the file. State your business.

speaker: Grimalkin
text: Sign me on as a field subject. Three engagements, logged.

speaker: Grimalkin
text: Another time.

speaker: Grimalkin

speaker: Grimalkin

speaker: Lift Attendant

speaker: Lift Attendant
text: About that crate.

speaker: Lift Attendant
text: The cage runs on the counterweight cycle. Down at the quarter bell, up at the half. You have four minutes, and I'll say so again at three.

speaker: Lift Attendant
text: Down at the quarter bell, up at the half. The Liscor news rode up on the same cycle as the tin did. I heard it four times before the cage reached the landing.

text: Which office starts it?

text: I'll find out.

speaker: Lift Attendant
text: The stamp clerk on the market tier holds the entry side. The permit window holds the release side. The consignee signs last. She cannot sign first. Down at the quarter bell.

speaker: Lift Attendant
text: Somebody should unstick that.

speaker: Lift Attendant
text: Then it waits.

text: Four cycles, and it will be five. The permit office holds the queue, and the office's own requisitions are sitting in that queue with everything else. Until their paper moves, nothing behind it moves, and nobody up there will sign out of order.

text: [The offices countersigned each other. It's released.]

speaker: Lift Attendant
text: [The exemption was in the forms the whole time.]

speaker: Lift Attendant
text: [I carried it down myself. It's on her dock.]

text: Still working on it.

speaker: Lift Attendant
text: Say it plainly. I have a cage to run in three minutes and I would like to run it happy.

speaker: Lift Attendant
text: Then the manifest is clean and the cage runs happy. Down at the quarter bell.

speaker: Lift Attendant
text: You carried it. Two tiers, on your own back, for a family that does not know your name. I have run this cage eleven years and watched a great many correct people wait. Ride free while I am on the gate, {addr}. That is the only thing I own to give.

speaker: Lift Attendant
text: You made the offices sign each other's paper. I am going to tell that story at every quarter bell for a month. The crate goes down on the next cycle, on top of the load.

speaker: Lift Attendant
text: It was in the forms. Four cycles, and it was in the forms. Do not speak to me until the half bell.

speaker: Lift Attendant
text: That's fairer than most of what I've heard.

speaker: Lift Attendant
text: It came up the shaft the way everything does, one voice at a time, each louder than the last. Liscor settled what was under its stone. The tier will talk about it for a week and then it will talk about tin again. The tin is four cycles late, {addr}. Liscor is two hundred miles away.

speaker: Lift Attendant
text: Give it a cycle.

speaker: Pisces

speaker: Pisces

speaker: Pisces
text: My team have annexed the corner by the fire and appear to consider the matter settled. I am here to observe the decline at close range. The fire is behaving. My rooms have a draft that comes in under the door, and I have moved the bed once already.

speaker: Pisces
text: The corner by the fire is empty and I am told I should feel some way about that. My team are off being strenuous somewhere unlit. I have declined to be strenuous with them, and the fire is still adequate.

speaker: Pisces
text: My team have reclaimed the corner by the fire and appear to consider the matter settled. I have taken the next table to observe the decline at close range. The fire is generous tonight. The rooms upstairs stay cold past midnight, and I have said so at the bar.

speaker: Pisces
text: "I'll leave you to your standards."

speaker: Pisces
text: Tavern fare is a solved problem. Salt and fat, applied in quantity until nobody thinks to ask a second question. I have eaten better in three cities. I have eaten considerably worse in nine. This kitchen I am still placing. I will want more bowls before I commit to a number.

speaker: Pisces
text: "I saw nothing. Precisely nothing."

speaker: Pisces
text: Hm. It is competent. I have called far worse things competent, and to far worse cooks. Though I observe that I have finished it, and I observe you observing.

speaker: Pisces
text: Wish me luck.

speaker: Pisces
text: Bleeding it is. Predictable, but effective. Go on, then. I shall be here with my notes. Do try to leave the frame intact.

speaker: Pisces
text: I'll take the compliment anyway.

speaker: Pisces
text: Hm. Correct. Aggravatingly correct. You have the eye, if not the training. Do not let it go to your head. The training is where the real work is.

speaker: Pisces
text: I'll take a look.

speaker: Pisces
text: Read it yourself, then. [Observe] the frame close, and mind that the pattern does not repeat the same way twice. Report back if you actually understand what you saw. I shall judge whether you do.

speaker: Pisces
text: Then it's settled. [Charming Smile]

speaker: Pisces
text: Actually - never mind.

speaker: Pisces
text: Then it's settled — I'll cover your time instead. (5 gold)

speaker: Pisces
text: A glance. Hm. If it truly reads as spatial and not necrotic, I could examine it without touching a thing. Fine — for the intellectual insult of not knowing. Do not mistake this for a favor.

speaker: Pisces
text: Thank you, Pisces.

speaker: Pisces
text: A spatial anchor. Crude. Fascinating. Whoever built your inn, adventurer, built it on something that remembers being elsewhere.

speaker: Pisces
text: It's not asking much. You'd know in a glance.

speaker: Pisces
text: Forget it, then.

speaker: Pisces
text: You want me to walk into someone's pantry and grope at a wild ward with my bare senses. No. I have wards of my own I would rather keep.

speaker: Pisces
text: Meet you at the door.

speaker: Pisces
text: Back to the top.

speaker: Pisces
text: Good. I have walked that gauntlet twice and marked the safe line myself, so we will not be dying of a flagstone. Bring your own rope. I am not carrying yours; I have a spine to preserve and a reputation that assumes I never lift anything.

speaker: Pisces
text: What do you expect to find?

speaker: Pisces
text: Not today.

speaker: Pisces
text: Three regions taught you the same word in three accents and not one of them noticed doing it. A witch feeds hers, milk and a word. An enchanter prices the draw and calls it craftsmanship. Pallass bills it as maintenance. Maintenance. Under this city is wardwork by the hand that cut our frame, and it has been drawing since before Liscor had walls. I want to read it standing in front of it.

speaker: Pisces
text: Your treatise said it in the third paragraph and I chose to admire the penmanship instead. Bound, fed, and waiting, with no term given. Three regions have since handed me the same word in three accents, and the hand that cut our frame cut the seal under this city. I want to read it standing in front of it.

speaker: Pisces
text: I'll think about it.

speaker: Pisces
text: Something that was fed on purpose, by people who expected to be dead long before it stopped needing feeding. Past that I have guesses, and I do not perform guesses in public. The honest answer is thinner than I would like.

speaker: Pisces
text: Sleep on it. Literally. Got it.

speaker: Pisces
text: Then the scholarship is done and the tedium begins. Keep both near the door, and rest. Rest is the instruction; I am aware of how it sounds. Attunement is a residency — the frame learns the stone the way a house learns its family: overnight, and more than once. Sleep. Let the inn do the part no [Mage] can rush.

speaker: Pisces
text: I'll clear whatever's coming through myself.

speaker: Pisces
text: Come look at it yourself. This is your kind of magic.

speaker: Pisces
text: I'll read the wardwork myself, then.

speaker: Pisces
text: A door that changes its mind about where it goes. How very like this city — even the fixtures have moods. You could bleed for my curiosity, if that is your instrument. You could attempt to talk me into caring, which has been done, rarely. Or prove you can read a ward without my help, and I will be forced to take you seriously. Choose, and do not waste my morning.

speaker: Pisces
text: East past the gate road. Understood.

speaker: Pisces
text: 'Indifferently cut.' You've been there?

speaker: Pisces
text: Then attend, because I dislike repeating myself. The door remembers being elsewhere; what it lacks is an anchor to remember by. East across the floodplains, well past the gate road, there is a seam of old dressed stone in the open grass — a ruin, collapsed and rude, but its plinth still cradles an anchor stone. Retrieve it. Krshia's resonant catalyst will attune the pairing. The ruin itself was indifferently cut before it ever collapsed. Mind the overhangs going in.

speaker: Pisces
text: On my way.

speaker: Pisces

text: Gone? Good. Dead? Better. The Watch is bricking that gallery before sundown — 'for now,' before you say it. Things under Liscor have a way of minding being sealed. The masons are already stacking brick, and they'll want the street clear. Good work. I mean it.

speaker: Zevara
text: The guard on the gate speaks well of you.

speaker: Zevara
text: (Back a step.)

speaker: Zevara
text: Ten years of long shifts. Six weeks of leave across all of them. Do the arithmetic and then don't ask why I look like this. My Senior Guardsmen are a spearmaster who won't stop talking and an Antinium I've heard maybe a dozen sentences from in two years. The wall stands. Ten years, no breach. I count that every morning, before the rosters.

speaker: Zevara
text: Then I'll go down.

speaker: Zevara
text: Give me a day to ready myself.

speaker: Zevara
text: There you are. A crew opening the grates under the market broke through into tunnels nobody dug. They go down, and they keep going. Olesm's maps say they shouldn't exist. I need somebody who isn't Watch to go and look. That's you.

speaker: Zevara
text: There you are. The cisterns crew found something under the new grates: tunnels nobody dug, going down past where their lanterns reached. Olesm's maps say they shouldn't exist. You've been down there. You're going again, this time for the Watch.

speaker: Zevara
text: Understood, Captain.

speaker: Zevara
text: On it.

speaker: Zevara
text: Good. See Olesm before you climb down. He's been up since the second bell drawing what shouldn't be there, and he'll want you carrying it. And take Relc. That's an order.

speaker: Zevara
text: A nest. Silver-backed spiders, up from the Dungeon. [Charming Smile]

speaker: Zevara
text: Actually — never mind.

speaker: Zevara
text: Here — three gold for the lanterns and the healer. Budget problem solved, at least. (3 gold)

speaker: Zevara
text: Before it's an emergency. Hm. You argue like someone who's read a casualty report. Fine. Make it plain. What am I actually sending them into?

speaker: Zevara
text: Under the city and moving, it's Watch business before it's an emergency. File after.

speaker: Zevara
text: Forget I asked.

speaker: Zevara
text: Sweep the cisterns. You know what a sweep costs? Six Watchmen off the wall, lanterns, a healer on standby, and a form in triplicate explaining to the Council why the wall was six thin. Give me one reason worth the ink.

speaker: Zevara
text: Appreciated.

speaker: Zevara
text: Spiders from the Dungeon. Wonderful. A nest that size costs me six Watchmen and a night of overtime. Consider it swept. I'll pull a squad at dusk and burn the silk out before it spreads. You did right bringing me a species and a location. Half the reports on my desk have neither. And good work. Now go tell whoever set you on this that the Watch has it.

speaker: Zevara
text: Appreciated.

speaker: Zevara
text: Set it on the desk. It goes down as lanterns and a healer. I'll pull a squad at dusk and burn the silk out, whatever's actually down there. Next time, bring me the count first.

speaker: Zevara
text: The scavengers off Market Street are dealt with.

speaker: Zevara
text: The cistern nest is gone. You know that one firsthand.

speaker: Zevara
text: The thing under the city. The big one.

speaker: Zevara
text: Nothing to claim yet.

speaker: Zevara
text: Good. The Watch posts standing bounties on anything that made a file cross my desk. You clear it and claim it here. I sign it. Keep the receipts honest. The Council audits the ledger every month.

speaker: Zevara
text: Anything else on the books?

speaker: Zevara
text: Captain.

speaker: Zevara
text: Signed. Mind the ink, it's still wet.

speaker: Zevara
text: The city's lucky it was you.

speaker: Zevara
text: (Back a step.)

speaker: Zevara
text: Understood, Captain.

speaker: Zevara
text: Somebody before me let things slide. Reports that went nowhere, as long as the dead were the kind the city didn't mourn. I wrote it up. Command found the paperwork inconvenient and the facts worse — and then the chair was mine. So no, I don't sleep much. The old reports are still in the cabinet behind my desk. Archiving them is a one-line requisition. I haven't written it.

speaker: Zevara
text: (Back a step.)

speaker: Zevara
text: Yes, Captain.

speaker: Zevara
text: Ten years of overtime is what that was. But — thank you. File it under 'said once.' Now get out of my gatehouse before I find you a shift.

speaker: Zevara
text: (Back a step.)

speaker: Zevara
text: Noted, Captain.

speaker: Zevara
text: Oldblood, yes. Fire, technically. Ten seconds of it, no air in my lungs the whole time, and a day of sounding like a gravel cart after. It's a weapon you pay for using, so I file it where I file all last resorts. You want fire that works, requisition a mage.

speaker: narrator
text: That's all I ask, Captain.
The fissure Zevara spoke of is down past the gallery. The dark has a direction today.
Somebody warded a way out of here before the passage was ever choked. The vein through it is the same coin-gold as the stones above.
Set into the wall beside the landing, older than the rubble and colder than the air. The frame of light under its surface answers the moment you look at it.
The rubble gives at your push — someone's already cleared a path through. The old gallery beyond is dark, but it is open.
Rubble and worked stone choke a passage that clearly led somewhere once. Someone sealed this side deliberately, and not long ago either.
The stone doesn't budge. Whatever's on the other side stays sealed. For now.
A carved shape crouches against the far wall, limbs folded, its eyeless face turned to the floor. It has not moved since you noticed it. That is the only reason you are still standing here.
You keep your distance. Whatever wakes it, you would rather not be the one who finds out.
Silk threads catch the light along the gallery's south wall, thick as rope, all leading back to one dark seam in the stone.
The spill shifts the moment you put weight on it and keeps shifting. Crossing that takes footing you have not got.
The doorway you came through, seen from the inside: the runes run the same order on this face, which means they were cut to be read from in here. Somebody expected to be standing where you are.
A waist-high plinth of the same pale stone as the ruin's, and the same hand's runes wrapped twice around it. Every line points inward. Whatever it holds, it was built to keep holding it.

Not a prisoner. An ANCHOR — a twin to the stone the Horns hauled out of the ruin, and it has been drinking the ward's slow pour for three centuries to stay awake. Pisces, hoarse: "This is why the Door works at all. Somebody left it something to come home to, and then somebody sealed the room and let it drink."
Someone knelt here long enough to cut a tally into the floor slab, and long enough after that to stop.
Cut into the slab, in a hand that expected readers: a tally. Ninety-one marks, then a gap, then one more in a different chisel. Nobody came back to make the ninety-third.
Quietly, if you can manage it. I have lost the count twice already and blamed you both times.
He has not sat down since you got here. One hand hovers a finger's width off the stone, tracking something along it that nobody else in the hall can see, and his lips move without sound.
Rubble and old wardwork still choke this side passage. Whatever's back there can wait until the main halls are actually safe.
A narrower passage breaks off from the gauntlet proper, half-choked with fallen stone. Small shapes move in the dark past the rubble — more than one.
The bones rise and fall into step behind you.
Old bones, settled where they fell. They are not going anywhere. Probably.
[Rope Work] — You make the line fast to the stub, drop the tail across, and set it taut. The crossing is a crossing now, and it stays one.
You get a hand on the stub and lean out. Nothing about that gap is jumpable, and nothing about the stub is climbable. What it wants is a rope.
A stub of masonry where a walkway used to leave this wall, sheared off clean. The other side is still there, four feet out and a long way down. The stub would hold a line all day.
The floor stops. You put a boot to the lip and gravel goes over the edge and keeps going. Not without something to hold.
The floor is simply gone here, one span of it, edge to edge. Dropped stone comes back as a sound and not much of one.
You get both hands under the edge and pull until your eyes swim. It rocks an inch and settles back. Heavier than you.
One slab off the ceiling, come down whole and standing on its edge across the gap in the wall. Its own weight is the only thing holding it there.
[Greater Strength] — You set your shoulder low, take the whole weight on your legs, and walk it aside. Stone grinds on stone and the gallery mouth stands open behind it.
Hauling at it idly will not do it. Setting your shoulder to it properly might.
A strapped case set down against the wall and never picked up again, the leather gone stiff and pale. Whoever put it there meant to come back through the span.
The straps give at a pull. Inside: chalk, a bent square, a coil of good wire, and five gold in a twist of cloth that somebody was saving for the walk home.
One flagstone sits a hair proud of its neighbors, the mortar cracked clean around its edge. Stepping square on it feels like a very bad idea.
The flagstone gives half an inch under your hand. Somewhere close, something CLICKS. Nothing else happens. This time.
A narrow slit runs along the wall at knee height, primed and waiting. Bare hands won't do it — you'd want a proper kit for this.
A narrow slit runs along the wall at knee height. Whatever is loaded behind it, you have no idea how to disable it.
You trace the mechanism with a careful eye, find the catch, and wedge it still with a wax-and-wire pick from the kit. The slit stays dark.
A narrow slit runs along the wall at knee height, primed and waiting. This wants a careful, deliberate touch, not a shove.
The floor ahead looks perfectly ordinary. Something about it still itches at the back of your mind.
You look again, and this time you see it: the grain runs the wrong way, and no dust has settled in months. That is not floor. That is a very good painting of floor.
The floor ahead looks exactly like the floor behind you. Somehow, that is the part that bothers you.
The stone here looks like all the other stone. It is not.
[Detect Magic] — The seam lights up like a badly kept secret: old wardwork, still holding, drawn tight around the floor ahead. Now you know exactly what not to trust.
Something under the stone hums off-key. Eyes that read mana could say what.
You give the wire a wide berth. Something in the dark past it has not noticed you yet.
A coil of taut wire lies strung ankle-height between two stones, near-invisible against the dust. Whatever it is rigged to is worse than a stubbed toe.
Whatever waits beyond this arch, you are not walking into it yet — not with the halls still armed, not without the Horns at your back.

The hall ends in a sealed archway, and beyond it something vast fills the dark almost completely — the same shape you glimpsed crouched near the entrance, closer now, utterly still. It is not still the way a statue is still.
The seal does not resist. It simply stops being a seal — the runes go quiet in order, one ring at a time, and the door swings in on three centuries of undisturbed air.

[Detect Magic] — Wardwork, and awake. It does not flare and settle the way a bound ward should. It holds one low steady note, like a breath nobody has to let out, and you have felt that note somewhere else.

[Detect Magic] — The ward opens under your sight and does not stop opening. It is not holding anything shut. It is POURING: one direction, one slow measured rate, into whatever the stone is between. It has poured since before the city. Pisces, very quietly: "Ah. So that is what the others were."

[Detect Magic] — Every reading you have taken lines up at once: the inn's frame, the ruin's socket, the seam back down the hall, the hollow west of Riverfarm. Not four wards. One lattice, and this door is where it drains to. Something behind this stone has been drinking Liscor's oldest work since before Liscor. Pisces uses a word you have never heard him use in public.

[Observe] — Worked stone, deliberate, and not one line of it reads like a lock. Whatever this door is for, it is not keeping people out. You would have to stand here longer, with someone who knows more than you do.

[Observe] — You take the runes in order, the way you would read a sentence. The turns repeat at a fixed interval. The pantry frame does exactly that, at exactly that interval, and this one is worn deeper: it has been doing it longer. Behind you, Pisces says nothing, which from him is applause.
The passage doesn't end here — it just goes quiet, past a bend the light doesn't reach. Whatever's back there, this isn't the moment.
The runes are the same. Not similar — the same hand, the same order, as the door in the inn's pantry.
Pisces reaches the door before you do and stops a handspan short of it. "The same hand. Not a school, not a fashion. A HAND, and it cut this one first." He does not look away while he says it.

Pisces steps back at last. "It is not a lock. The lines run one way, they have run one way for a very long time, and something on the far side has been drinking the whole while. Your inn has a frame by this hand. Sleep well."
The runes keep their slow one-way order. Pisces has stopped narrating and started counting under his breath, which is worse.
Dust lies on it in an unbroken sheet, the way dust lies on a thing that has not moved in centuries. Leave it that way.
An alcove beside the sealed door, and something standing in it: ward-stone, shoulder-high, cut in the same hand as the runes. It is not a statue. Statues are not built facing the door they guard.
Road's watched. You're welcome.
Heh. Alright, alright - I like you. You've got the look of someone who buys a guy a drink after. We're good, you and me. Best guardsman in Liscor says so.
A Drake built like a barracks door, spear worn smooth from use, standing at ease the way only dangerous people stand. He watches the road and everyone on it. Including you, now.
Straw and burlap lashed to posts, hacked half to ribbons. Someone drills here often, and hard. The stitching tells you where a real guard would break.
Relc whistles. "Not bad for a start. Now go SLEEP on it — Classes come at the pillow, not the podium. Bed's upstairs at the inn."
A cairn on a hill. The view is mostly weather.
[Eagle Eyes] — The plains resolve: the gate road, the ruin east past it, and every fold of dead ground a warband could hide in. You'll walk this land differently now.
From up here the floodplains pretend to be a map. Good eyes could read it.
The seam splits wider at your touch, cold air breathing out of the dark beneath. You step through, into somewhere else.
A hairline crack runs through old, dressed stone half-swallowed by turf — not natural rock, something built. Cold air breathes up out of it, and it smells of somewhere else.
A cold seam splits the earth here, sealed by old stone. It doesn't feel like it goes anywhere. Yet.
Three boulders sit too evenly spaced for the hillside's own tumble, and one of them, you'd swear, just shifted.
The crab regards you with all the tameable warmth of a boulder.
Nothing moving out there. Whatever it was keeps day hours, same as everyone sane.
A patrol slipping the boulder line, quiet until they're not. Only after dark.
A shape stands too still at the treeline, antlers catching a warmth that isn't sunlight.
A scrape of trampled grass, two long-beaked shapes hunched low over it, watching you watch them.

A corusdeer, down in the grass with a leg it won't put weight on. Its antlers barely glow. It watches you the way anything hurt watches anything larger. It would let patient hands close, and hands that tend enough hurt beasts learn something no drill yard teaches.
[Beast's Mending] — Splint and salve, and the leg sits straighter than it has any right to. The corusdeer breathes easier.
[Beast's Mending] — The splint comes away and stays away. It stands, tests the leg, and goes to find the herd. Your hands knew what to do because of this deer.
It has let you close once today. Don't spend what little trust it has.
You move slow, keep your hands low, and it lets you check the leg. That, from a wild thing, is everything.
It knows you now. It holds still while you work, and its antlers warm the air between you.
It is already standing when you come. It lets you run a hand down the leg once, then turns and goes up the rise at a trot, and does not look back.
A body-shaped hollow pressed into the grass, going green again at the edges. Something lay here a long time, and then stopped needing to.
In the flattened grass, shed clean at the base: one antler, oaken-brown fading to a red glow at the tip. It is warm to hold, and stays warm.
Only the hollow in the grass now, and it is filling in.
The pup sniffs your hand once, twice — then leans its whole small weight against your leg. That's that, then.
The pup shrinks back. You don't have the hands for this yet — hands like that are learned on hurt animals, one at a time. There's a corusdeer down in the grass east of here that would let you start.
A scrape under the boulder line, and in it one wolf pup, ribs showing, too young to be alone. The pack that left it is not coming back.
It watches your hands. Whatever you mean to offer it, offer it properly.
It bites you exactly once, decides you took it well, and climbs your sleeve to glare at the horizon from a better vantage.
It snaps at your fingers. Fair enough. Nothing wild takes an offer from hands that have never tended anything.
A razorbeak chick, blown or chased from the nest scrape, hissing at the whole world from behind a tussock. The nest is close. The parents are not.
It stops hissing when you crouch. Interested, then — if you make the offer the right way.
It walks out of the scrape without being asked and stands on your foot. The pack keeps its own counsel about who leaves with whom.
The pup watches you the way it watches weather. Hands that can take an offer like this are learned on hurt animals, one at a time.
The scrape under the boulder line has been dug out again and re-lined. A season on, and there is a pup in it: bolder than the last one, and entirely unimpressed by you.
It has not learned to be afraid of hands yet. Make the offer before it does.
It stalks the length of your arm, finds the shoulder acceptable, and settles there facing backwards. Somebody has to watch the way you came.
It flares its hackles and holds the tussock. Nothing wild takes an offer from hands that have never tended anything.
The nest scrape has fledged another. This one has already worked out that the tussock is cover and that you are not, and it is holding both facts against you.
It goes still when you crouch, which from a razorbeak is an invitation. Make the offer properly.
It leans, the way the first one leaned. You are not being given a replacement. You are being given another one.
The pup does not move. Hands that can take an offer like this are learned on hurt animals, one at a time.
Late in the season and thin with it, but another scrape further down the boulder line is occupied. Whatever else the floodplains do, they keep doing this.
It is too tired to flinch. Offer, and mean it.
The small figure on the rise watches you. It does not move to meet you.
A small figure on the rise south, standing very still. It has been watching you for a while, and it wants you to know that.
You go down between the stones sideways, the way the flattened grass says to, and the plains close over the top of you.
Two low stones lean together where the ground folds away, and the grass between them is beaten flat by small feet. Smoke comes up thin and does not spread.
The road's empty in the daylight. Whatever works this verge keeps to the dark.
Two heavy shapes working the verge of the wagon road, wings folded tight, close enough to the carter camps to smell the fires. Only after dark.
A scatter of old bones the wolf will not leave alone. It noses through them, circles, noses again, and looks back at you as though the next part is your job.
You dig where the wolf keeps insisting. Under the bones, wrapped in rotted cloth: a charm on a cord gone soft with age.
Turned bones and nothing under them now. The wolf has lost interest, which is its own verdict.
A boulder standing clear of the reeds with the whole pond below it. The razorbeak keeps climbing it and screaming at the water, which is either an opinion or a report.

It wheels out over the pond, hangs, and comes back loud. There is something square and man-made on the bottom, a stride out from the bank — too far to reach across open water, and water can be made to bear weight.
The meat is good and it will not stay good. Raw and cold, it is no use to you, and you have no way to change that.

A young corusdeer down in the grass with its neck wrong, cold hours ago and not yet found by anything with teeth. The hide is whole. The haunches are worth carrying, if you had a way to make them keep.
[Flame Jet] — You run the lance along the haunch until the fat goes loud and the outside blackens. You cut what will travel and leave the rest to the grass.
Hauling at it with your hands gets you nothing. Fire is what this wants.
The paint is newer than the post it hangs on. Somebody meant it, and means it still.
A hand-painted board, letters gone bold where they were traced twice: THE WANDERING INN — NO KILLING GOBLINS.
Whatever's under there won't come to bare hands. Lism's shelf had a fisher's handline.

The pond narrows here over a drop the light doesn't reach. Every so often the water moves wrong, and then it stops, the way a room stops when you walk into it. Whatever keeps this water is not interested in being caught.
The water's gone still. Whatever considered you today is done considering.
You pay out the line into the dark water. Nothing takes it, and nothing was ever going to — whatever keeps this pool knows the difference between an offer and a hook.

Something square and man-made rests on the pond floor a stride out from the bank, furred with silt. Too far to reach across open water. But water can be made to bear weight, if you know the trick of cold.

Kneeling on the ice, you lever the silt-caked strongbox free. Drake-work, old, its lock long rusted through. Inside, dry against all odds, a few keepsakes someone drowned here meant never to be found.
The strongbox sits open and empty now, holding nothing but pond-light.
Scree slides out from under your boot and rattles away down the slope. Getting up that needs surer feet than yours.

A ring of river stones with a fire kept deliberately small. Someone has banked it low and swept the ash back, so the smoke goes up thin instead of out wide. Nothing about this fire wants to be seen from the road.
The wood is sorted by burn time in three piles. Somebody in this camp thinks two nights ahead.
Green hides pegged out on a lattice of spear-shafts, scraped down to nothing on one side. The pegs are all different lengths, whittled to fit whatever the rack needed that day.
Every hide is stretched to the same tension. Whoever runs this rack does not let anyone else near it.
A flat stone at the high end of the hollow, worn smooth in one small patch. It faces the way in. There is no cushion, no cover, and nothing near enough to hide behind.
From here you can see the cut in the turf, the fire, and everyone's hands at once. It was not chosen for comfort.
A shoulder yoke cut for someone half your height, propped against a stack of empty baskets. The baskets go out full and come back full of something else.
The baskets are all out. Nothing left to haul until they come back.
You shorten the yoke by two notches and spend the morning hauling water and cut brush. Somebody presses coin into your hand at the end without looking up.
The yoke has been left out on your side of the fire. Nobody says anything about it, and nobody moves it back.
A goblin sitting where the light from the cut in the turf lands, sharpening something that is already sharp. It has not looked directly at you once.
A rack of split poles standing empty over a bed of ash. The hunters look north at the range, and then back at it, and say nothing.
The poles are bare and the ash is cold. Hands on the camp's baskets first, the old one signs at you, and then something big brought down off the range north.
You hang what you brought back and cut it down thin the way the old one shows you, and by the time the light goes the rack is heavy for the first time this year.
The poles are bowed under strips cut thin and even, and the ash beneath has been banked warm to hold the smoke in them.
Nobody moves the rack aside when you pass it now.
Three of them stand on the lip of the hollow where it is easiest to come down, looking at the racks and doing arithmetic. Nobody in the camp is pretending not to have noticed.
The stonework is older than the door you came through, and the pose is a dancer's, not a soldier's. Someone carved joy here, and meant it to last.
Cool spray beads on the stone. The statue's face is worn soft — whoever it was, the water remembers them better than the carving does.
Someone carried a real bed out here, onto real grass, under a sky that isn't real. It's made up with clean linen anyway, like that settles the argument.
Somewhere, a door shuts softly. The garden doesn't dim.
A stone plinth, swept clean, facing the axis like the others. Whatever belongs here hasn't been carried up from below yet.

A gnoll carved in stone, sword low and steady, facing down toward where the path forgets itself. Something old came up from under Liscor once. Something else went down after it, and came back up alone. The warren has been quiet since.
An empty plinth near the row's center, the mist pooling faintly at its base as if it expects company.

A drake in stone, spear planted, watching over ground that used to worry the whole city. Liscor sealed the dark for good, once the warren was cleared — masonry over memory, and no one asked for thanks. This is as close as the hill gets to giving one anyway.
A stone plinth at the far end of the row, otherwise unremarkable, waiting on whatever the inn hasn't settled yet.
A human figure in stone, apron tied, a bowl held out in both hands like an offering that never quite finished being made. The inn came up short once. Nobody outside its walls ever had to know.
A bare stone plinth at the end of the row, angled slightly wide of the others — room left on purpose. Nothing stands on it yet. The mist doesn't seem to mind waiting.
A goblin carved in stone, unarmed, hands open at its sides. Not every ending here was a fight. This one is remembered for not being one.
Welcome to The Wandering Inn! Mind giving that table a wipe?
Oh - hi! You've got a good face, you know that? Come in, sit down. I'll find you something warm - on the house, probably. Don't tell Lyonette I said that.
A young human, no armor, no weapon, no idea she is the strangest thing in this world. She moves like someone still deciding to be brave. The inn already leans toward her.
I am not queueing. I happen to be seated near where a queue would form.
I am not queueing. I happen to be seated near where a queue would form.
Off shift. Good chair, good fire. The wall can hold itself up for one night.
Nobody has found me yet. Do not be the one who does.
Nobody has found me yet. Do not be the one who does.
Off duty. I am told this is a thing a person can be.
Warm here. Two doors. I counted.
Evening, {addr}. No business tonight, you'll be glad to hear.
Sit down properly if you are going to sit.
The tables are covered. Nothing more to carry out until tomorrow.
You carry the laden tray out to the tables.
Mind the floors, they're just done.
Lyonette's chin lifts, then softens despite itself. You're kind. People are not, usually, to the help. ...It is a small thing. It is not nothing. Sit where you like; I'll bring something hot.
A human girl playing at composure a size too large for her. Her hands know trays; her chin knows courts. The two have not finished arguing.
The kettle wants yarrow before it gives anything back.
A kettle, singing low. It's just a kettle, unless you know otherwise.
[Hedge Remedy] — The inn's kettle does in a pinch, just like she said. The steam settles into something kinder.
The kettle's on. The inn won't mind one more thing brewing, so long as it means well.
A working counter, scrubbed and stocked. The kitchen has standards, and they're looking at you.
[Advanced Cooking] — Knife-work first, then the pan, then the part nobody can teach. The plate comes out arguing for seconds.
Good stock, better knives, and nobody using either. A real cook could turn this counter into a meal worth naming.
The good copper pan, hung out of easy reach. Erin's rule, probably.
[Signature Dish] — The pan remembers you now. What comes out of it isn't dinner, it's a reputation.
The good copper pan. It's been waiting for a dish that deserves it.
You don't know your way around a stew pot. Yet.
[Basic Cooking] — The stew comes out rich and hot.
The stew's at the turn. Someone who knows a pot could bring it home.
The order's a mess and you haven't the first idea how to stretch it. Not yet.
[Basic Cooking] — You thin the stock, fold in day-old bread, and stretch the short order into a full service. Lyonette's shortfall vanishes into the pot.
Three plates ordered, one pot of stock. You could stretch it to cover them all. Nothing leaves the kitchen in your hands.
A plain plank door, warped at the bottom from a hundred winters. Nothing about it looks like it goes anywhere but the pantry.
The frame and the old marks under its paint both want a trained eye — and maybe more than one kind.
[Detect Magic] — The old wardwork wakes just enough to be read: someone bound this cellar's door long before it learned to go elsewhere.

[Observe] — The grain of the frame isn't grain at all: a pattern worked into the wood, old and deliberate, repeating around the jamb like a held breath. It doesn't move while you watch it. It moves the instant you look away.
Onions, a sack of soft potatoes, a shelf of jarred somethings gone dusty. The pantry door, same as it's always been.
The find leans against the pantry frame, unhung, with the old plank door stacked out of the way behind the flour sacks. Pisces has not stopped circling it since the wagon. Ask him about it.
A moment. I am counting the ward's repeats, and you are extremely countable.

He has taken his coat off, which for Pisces is manual labour. One hand rests flat on the hauled door's face, the way a physician rests a hand on a patient, and he is listening to something no one else in the room can hear.
Something scratches behind the pantry wall, patient and small. Probably nothing. Probably.
The scratching has become a chewing. The Door strains for somewhere it cannot reach yet, and something on the way there has found the gap and has teeth.
The vines part like a curtain, and the light beyond doesn't flicker.
Plaster, old and thin, and a nail with nothing hung on it. If something is meant to be here, it isn't yet.
Bare wall. A nail with nothing hung on it.
A door of living vines, woven shut and breathing faintly of green. It wasn't here before, and it doesn't pretend otherwise.
[Basic Cleaning] — The table is spotless.
The table's a mess of rings and crumbs. It wants a proper wipe-down.
Ask me about the vault again and I'll start charging Pisces rent.
My arm's still fine.
I am still counting exits. There are still two.
Ask me about the vault again and I'll start charging Pisces rent.
My arm's still fine.
I am still counting exits. There are still two.
The inn's room register, open to today. Lyonette's handwriting could win awards; the prices underneath it could start fights.
Faded arcane script. You can't read a word of it. Whoever penned this knew magic you don't. Someone in the city must.

With what Pisces beat into you, the faded script stops being noise: it is a warding treatise, old and patient, and it keeps circling one subject. A door. Bound, sealed, and fed — somewhere close. He would want to see this.
[Light] — A steady white orb settles into the lantern's glass.
The wick's dry and ready. All it wants is a light that doesn't need a match.
Innkeeper! Anyone?
Off the clock, for once. Don't tell the Guild I remember how to sit down.
The market can keep until morning. A good bowl and a warm fire, yes?
One night off. I have already mapped every exit twice. It is a sickness.
The hall on the other side, and a bolt on this side. The bolt is most of what the lease bought.
Made up tight, corners squared. Lyonette did that, and she will know if you undo it badly.
Your own room, and a door you can shut behind you.
Your own room, and bedding aired for you rather than for whoever comes next.
Your own room, the best bedding in the house, and a shut door between you and all of Liscor.
Your own footlocker. Nothing in it yet that needs a key.
A plain footlocker at the head of the bed, hasp and no lock. Everything you own would rattle around in it.
The desk is yours to use. Nothing on it yet is asking to be done.
A narrow desk under the window, one drawer, and a pale ring where somebody set a cup down for a whole winter.
Nothing on the shelves yet. Give it a season.
Three shelves and you have filled none of them. Depending on the hour that is a sad thing or a hopeful one.
You hang the day's coat and it stays hung. It is a small thing and it is not nothing.
Pegs worn pale at the shoulder height of forty travellers who hung a coat here and went away again.
Nothing there — just your own four walls, and the particular quiet of a room nobody else is paying for.
The key turns like it has been waiting to. Your room, and nobody else's.
It doesn't budge.
Shut, and the card slot in the frame is empty. Somebody paid for this one once and stopped.
Your name in the card slot, in Lyonette's ruled hand, and the key for it somewhere in your pack.
It doesn't budge.
Your own bed.
Your own bed, and a mattress that no longer remembers the last guest.
Your own bed, thick blankets, and a shutter that actually closes.
Your own room, warm and quiet, with a bed you are almost sorry to leave.
Locked. Lyonette keeps exactly one door in this inn that isn't anyone's business but hers.

Lyonette's door, shut the way she shuts most things: completely, and without discussion. Whatever the room looks like behind it, you'll have to imagine it; she's not one to leave doors, or herself, half open.
A coat over the chair back, good cloth, nobody in it. The table has two cups and one of them has been sitting there since before you arrived.
You set it down on a table nobody has claimed and it sits there being a package. Behind you a chair turns a quarter inch, so you pick it back up.
The coat is already over the chair back. You lay yours beside it, take the wrong one on the way past, and nobody in this room has raised a voice or an eye.
Two men at the far table are having a conversation you are not in. Tonight, that is all they are.
Two men at the far table who arrived together, ordered separately, and have been agreeing with each other about nothing for an hour.

entity.display_name: A Woman Who Came in a Carriage

text: Gloves still on indoors, a chair chosen for its view of the door, and nothing at all on the table in front of her. She has been served and has not touched it.
He keeps the ledger of who is owed a table rather than who is owed money, which in this house is the more delicate book. He has not written anything down since you came in.

entity.display_name: A Gnoll with a Bad Ankle

text: Boot off, ankle up on the bench, and a bowl of something going cold while she tells the story properly rather than quickly.
A full cup, untouched, at his right hand, and his chair turned three degrees off the table so he can see both doors without turning his head.
Built for a bigger room than this one, and kept fed accordingly. The chairs nearest it are the worst chairs in the house and they are always taken.
Bows, a cracked buckler, one very good spear. Nothing here was donated. Every piece was left behind by somebody who did not come back for it, and the house does not say which.
Elbow-polished to a shine along its whole length except one arm's width at the far end, which is somebody's, permanently.
Long enough for a full company and set for four. The house leaves it that way on purpose, and everybody in the room has noticed and nobody mentions it.
Names in three columns, and a fourth column with no heading. The fourth column is shorter than it was last season and nobody has rubbed it out.
Nine pegs. Eight have hats. The third from the left is empty and has been wiped, which is not the same as being unused.
You hang your hat on the third peg, brim out, the way the house does it. Across the room a man you have not looked at stops not looking at you.
A keg with a tapped face and an honest week's dents.
Its brother. Slightly fuller, slightly further from the door.
Coppers, a dog-eared deck, and chalk tallies in three different handwritings. The game never quite ends; it just changes players.
The wobbly one. Guests get it first.
The good stool. You'd have to earn it.
Banded oak, twice-locked, sitting where the quiet gentleman can count who looks at it.
Locked twice over. The quiet gentleman clears his throat, courteously.
Ledgers with no titles and boxes with no labels. Everything here is filed under later.
Army-neat. Whoever sleeps here folds corners like it still matters.
Less neat. A paperback under the pillow, spine broken at the same chapter.
Hats on pegs, every one accounted for. House rule says they stay on. Nobody explains the exceptions, and nobody asks twice.
Evening, {addr}. Fine weather for good behavior.
He inclines the hat half an inch — a genuine courtesy, not a performance of one. "A pleasure," he says, and seems to mean it.
A Gnoll in a vest cut sharper than his manners need to be, tall hat squared like it's holding a rank. He watches the room's exits before he watches you.

A slate by the cots, chalked in two hands: addresses with no names against them, times with no dates, and a column of initials down the edge. Small work. The Brothers keep the small work moving because the small work is how they hear things.
The slate is wiped clean. Come back when the chalk's been busy.
You take the top line off the slate and walk it across Invrisil: a package nobody described to you, to a door somebody did. Two gold, and the line is wiped before you're back through the alley.
Marker-holder's rate. The line you take is longer, the door further out, and nobody asks you to account for the way round you took getting there.
Even a couch here fits like it was fitted for you. The Brothers do nothing halfway, not even hospitality.
A person of discernment, Wilovan said. I withdraw one full half of my suspicions.
A short Drake in careful browns, floppy cap settled down over the neck-spines. His eyes did your full inventory the moment you stepped in, and he's too polite to say what it came to.
A broad man in a bowler hat, playing solitaire like the deck owes him money. Politely, though.
A Gnoll with a folded coat over one arm, keeping polite company with the hat stand and the door.
A Drake on a stool with his back to the wall, minding the shelf and the chest the way other men mind a fire.
A drink counter kept cleaner than the law would ever ask it to be.
Rings from a hundred glasses, sanded out and earned back.
Bottles arranged by loyalty rather than label. The top row is for after jobs that went well.
The Liscor stones were rougher. This one has been handled by people with better manners; it barely shows the wear.
A plain grey stone, out of place against the marble — until you notice the coin-gold vein running through it, and the frame of light waiting just under the surface.
Plum silk, a little too fine for the errand she's running. She counts her change twice.
Plum silk a season past its moment, worn on an errand that plainly sits beneath it. She counts the change twice and does not hide the second count.
A Gnoll traveler, tan road-cloak, watching the crowd the way a stranger watches weather.
A tan road-cloak with the dust still in the weave, and a Gnoll under it reading the crowd the way you would read weather coming.
Stacked shipping crates, waist-high, the kind of cover a man leans on to watch a street without looking like he's watching it.

You circle the block twice before it clicks: the modest COYLE AND SONS sign out front doesn't match the two wagons idling round the side, or the men counting crates like men who've been shorted before. Whatever Coyle's really running out of, the front door is the least of it.
A runner ducks out Coyle's side door with a ledger under one arm, moving with the particular haste of someone who'd rather not be noticed leaving.
You fall in a comfortable distance behind. The runner doesn't loop, doesn't double back — just walks like a man with somewhere specific to be, heading for the alleys off the boulevard's east end.
Nothing under the colonnade but shadow. Whoever works this corner keeps night hours only.
Two shapes peel off the shadowed colonnade, unhurried, the way people move when they've done this before. Only after dark.
A chalked ring on the cobbles, two of Coyle's regulars leaning against the wall beside it, already sizing you up.
Panes racked like coins on edge. The glazier watches the street through his own stock, which is either pride or advertising.
Boots on pegs, sorted by wear. The pair in the window has walked to Pallass and back, if the sign is honest. Signs here mostly are.
Three tables, steam on the glass, and a chalk line of prices that assumes you already know what smoke-leaf costs in Invrisil.

A modest hanging board, burgundy and brass, lettered COYLE AND SONS in a hand that cost more than the paint. The frontage behind it is one narrow door and a clean window. Everything that actually moves through this firm goes round the side, on wagons, after dark.
Slate roofs and chimney smoke. The city keeps its second story to itself.
[Eagle Eyes] — The rooftop line resolves into a second city: runners' shortcuts, a watcher over Coyle's block, and two gentlemen who are always politely elsewhere.
The rooftops run straighter than the streets. Somebody up there knows it.

Ruled paper in three weights, ink in four, and a card offering a scribe by the hour in a hand that is itself the advertisement. Half the contracts argued about on this street were bought here first, quietly, by both sides.

Every front on this stretch has stopped pretending to be busy. A wheel-track runs through the wet marble, wider than a trade wagon lays and far too clean, and it is already curving away three streets north.
Pink lacquer, gone before you turned your head. The boulevard takes a moment to remember it was doing something, and nobody on it says the name out loud.

A gap in the row of shopfronts, three strides wide and going darker the further in it goes. A stride past the wall line the paving changes underfoot, boulevard marble to whatever the alleys were laid with.
A house sign with no name on it, only a hand of cards face down and a hat on a peg. Half the silver in this city drinks here and none of it says so out loud.
Browsing, or selling?
He offers a smile with the price tag still visible on the underside. "Charming," he allows, in the tone of a man crossing an item off a ledger.
Coin-gold trim on a merchant's collar, rings enough to case a fist. He totals you before you've said a word — cheaply, by the look on his face.
A woman in a rose-dyed cloak checks a folded slip of paper against a shopfront number, unimpressed by both.
She holds the slip at arm's length, then the shopfront number, then the slip again. Whatever address she was given, this street declines to be it.
Blue-grey wool, city cut. She doesn't look at you. Nobody here looks at anybody.
Blue-grey wool, cut the way this city cuts it, and a walking pace she has no intention of breaking for you or anyone.
A porter's barrow, half-unloaded, and a man in no hurry to finish the other half.
The barrow is half empty and he is in no hurry about the other half. He has the arms for a faster day and has decided against one.
Olive work clothes, ink-stained cuffs. A clerk between one ledger and the next.
Olive work clothes, ink to the second knuckle, and a satchel worn flat on one side from the same walk every day.
Mustard-brown coat, city boots, the specific walk of a man pretending he isn't lost.
Mustard-brown coat, good city boots, and the specific unhurried circling of a man who will not be asking anybody.
The crate stack looks ordinary until you notice the angle: top-heavy, wedged to fall. Pulling from the bottom feels like a very bad idea.
You brace the stack and ease the wedge free by hand. Behind the bottom crate: a couple of coins someone forgot to collect.
Cleaned out — by you, earlier. The alley keeps its own inventory schedule.
A stack of crates wedged just wrong, top-heavy and set to come down on whoever pulls from the bottom. Old footpad mischief.
A back-alley apothecary's bench, crowded with someone else's half-finished work. None of it means anything to you.
Shelves of labelled jars, a rented burner, and a hand-lettered card: WORKING SPACE, BY THE HOUR, NO CREDIT.
[Low-Grade Synthesis] — Someone else's burner, your working. The draught comes out crude but honest, same as anywhere.
A cramped apothecary corner, its burner free for anyone who knows the working. Invrisil rents everything by the hour, including this.
A severe man at a spotless corner bench, tools laid out at right angles. Everything about him says the prices are exact and the opinions are free.

entity.display_name: A Back Door with a Ledger Behind It

text: A back door with no handle on this side. Nothing about it is any of your business tonight.

entity.display_name: A Back Door with a Ledger Behind It

text: A door with no handle on this side and a fresh scrape where somebody's boot goes when their hands are full. The ledger inside is worth more than the stock.

entity.display_name: A Back Door with a Ledger Behind It

text: The Fence's strongbox gives up a lady's stone — forty years missing and still warm with someone else's guilt. It goes in your pack like it weighs more than it does.

entity.display_name: A Man with a Rented Table

text: A folding table rented by the day, a cloth over it, and a brass block sitting on the cloth with two letters cut into the face. He has not covered it, because covering a thing is how a street learns you have one.
Two men paid by the week whether they work or not, and plainly out of practice.
You take the brass off the cloth yourself. Two letters, cut deep, and a table with nobody left standing beside it.
Tea's free. Rumor's a gold the cup.
She pours you a cup without being asked. "On the house," she says, "which is the only kind of trade I ever regret."
A tea-tray harness worn shiny at the left shoulder — she pours right-handed and listens left-eared. The cups are chipped. The ears are not.
Two figures loitering with the specific stillness of people about to stop pretending they're not waiting for you.
The second pair, closer to the counting-house door — same trick, same stillness, better light to see it by.
The desk's own ledger reads clean, which is exactly the kind of clean a man pays for. You don't have the eye to find the real one. Not yet.

The desk's own ledger reads clean — too clean, the kind of clean a man pays for. Whatever's real is hidden better than this. You'll want to know how this place is watched before you go digging further.

[Appraise Foe] — Now you know the gap in the watch, the true ledger comes easy: tucked behind a false-backed drawer no honest desk needs. Forty gold to a 'removal man,' dated the night before Coyle's own theft: his hand, his numbers, his mistake. The drawer's second catch gives up a shallow hidden safe behind it, empty now but scored where something heavier than coin sat until recently.
The clean ledger is the tell. Sizing up what is really here takes a practiced read.
Two men on the door, pacing something. You don't have the eye to time it yet.

[Appraise Foe] — Two men on the counting-house door, and they're sloppier than they think: the same slow circuit, the same gap while both backs are turned, near enough on the bell to set a watch by. Time it right and the desk inside is yours for a minute, maybe two.
Two men keep the counting-house door. Sizing up their rhythm takes a practiced read.
The runner's trail ends at a side door with fresh boot-scuff on the sill and burgundy-and-brass livery moving past the gap in the shutters. Coyle's crew, and no mistaking the building now.
The runner ducks inside, and you finally see the whole of it: crates stacked to the rafters, more of Coyle's livery than a legitimate warehouse ever needs. Wherever the come-along ends, it ends here.
Three men in burgundy-and-brass doublets, clubs and knives held like men who've used them before. Merchant-livery, not Watch steel — Coyle's, all the way down to the stitching.
A taut line crosses the alley at ankle height, tied off crate to drainpipe. It's clearly meant to trip someone. You can't see how to clear it safely.
You unhook the line and coil it loose. A couple of coins sit tucked in the crate it was tied to, payment nobody came back to collect.
The stash spot sits empty. Knowing this alley, someone will restock it.
A snag-line at ankle height, tied crate to drainpipe. Old footpad work, the kind meant to trip a running mark. Worth clearing.
Banked low, kept alive all day. Paper hates damp and this street sits in the river's breath every morning.

entity.display_name: A Lady with a Ring Box

text: She has taken the chair furthest from the window and put a small hinged box on the table in front of her, closed. She has not opened it once in the time you have been standing here.
Cuffs pinned back, three nibs laid out in order of nerve, and the particular stillness of a man who is paid to have heard nothing.
Three weights, stacked lightest at the top, each with its price chalked on the edge of the shelf rather than the stock. Nothing here is priced where you can carry the number away.
Four inks, and the fourth is twice the price of the third for a difference you can only see in daylight. Somebody in this city has bought it every week for years.
Worn smooth in one narrow band where a hundred people a week have leaned to sign something they had already decided to sign.
A brass bell nobody rings, a blotter, and a small mirror angled so the man behind the counter can watch the door without appearing to.
Nine colours of wax and one blank seal for hire. The blank is the most used thing in the shop, by a distance.
Printed forms with the terms left open, sorted by how badly the second party will want to argue later. The thickest stack is the most reasonable-looking one.
A desk set at an angle that lets the scribe see the street and the street see nothing. There is a second chair, and it has been sat in recently.
Barracks is Watch business only. State yours.
A belt-slate at his hip, chalk stub worn to a nub, already a line into today's tally. Rust-brown scales, no plate for a desk posting — he'd rather be finishing the count than talking to you.

Tidier than her schedule allows. A stack of gate-shift reports pinned under a paperweight shaped vaguely like a threat. She is almost never behind it. The gate keeps her busier than her own office does.
Watch Captain's desk. Empty, same as every other time you've walked past it.
Barred, and empty behind the bars. You can tell by the quiet. Whatever ends up in here hasn't happened yet.
A single holding cell, iron-barred, straw swept into one corner. Duty-mundane, like everything else in this building — until it isn't.
Nothing to shoot with. A bow in hand would do it.
A straw-packed target lashed to a post, set against the wall where a stray shot won't find a person. Scored through in a tight cluster, more or less — somebody here takes the drills seriously.
You have shot your quiver dry for today. The straw will keep.
You put an arrow in the straw. Not bad, for someone who still flinches at the draw.
A second kit crate, shoved into the corner and never reshelved. The sergeant's own tally probably missed it.
A folded half-letter, tucked behind a loose board. Someone started writing it and never finished.
A scrap of paper pinned low, tucked behind a loose board same as the letter across the room.
Nothing there. Stone, kit racks, and the smell of oil worked into wood over years.
Nothing there. A shield knocks against its peg down the corridor, then goes quiet.
Adventurers. Always tracking mud in.
...Huh. You're actually pleasant. That's rare on this side of the counter. Fine - your paperwork jumps the line today. Don't make it weird.
A Drake behind a counter she clearly wishes were taller. Tired, sharp, quick with a ledger. She has sized up a hundred adventurers today and found most of them wanting.

TRAVELER'S NOTE, pinned crooked. Village called Riverfarm, downriver a fair walk, farming folk, growing fast under some new lord. They've got witch trouble, or so the last one through here said — crops going bad, nobody saying why out loud. No bounty on it, just word passed along. Ask the Guild about the road if you're curious.

A LETTER, sealed in wax gone slightly soft from handling, addressed to no one by name. Inside: impeccable handwriting regrets to inform you of a small disagreement in Invrisil concerning a mutual acquaintance's good name, and would consider it a personal favor — and a professional one — if a stranger to the city might look into it. The witch at Riverfarm keeps the stones, should the distance prove an obstacle. Signed only with a small drawing of a hat. The Guildmistress's clerk says it arrived by very ordinary post, which is itself the strangest part.

A WATCH NOTICE, freshly pinned. The reopened gallery under the old seal is to be surveyed properly before the Council calls it settled — volunteers with Guild standing should see Olesm Swifttail at the frontage desk. Pay is Watch-scale. The notice does not say what 'properly' means, and nobody pinning notices ever does.
WATCH NOTICE, pinned by a hand in a hurry. Recruit Pell missed second muster running. Ashgrave's not calling it desertion, not yet. Anyone with eyes free, ask at the barracks.

A SCRAP OF PARCHMENT, tacked low, easy to miss. 'LOST: one backup warhammer, plain steel, no love lost between us but I want it back. Ask for Renn. Reward for the honest sort.' The handwriting gets angrier toward the bottom.
Rates set by the Guild. Complaints to the Guildmistress in person. Bring patience. — S.S.
The Request Board. Your slip is still logged at the desk. The board does not care how it's going.

The Request Board. Paper three layers deep, new notices pinned straight over the dead ones. A posting pays on turn-in; take one at the Guildmistress's desk so it's logged, and only what you do after counts.

Handbills and scraps overlapping the request board's edge. The Guild's actual business spills past its own furniture. Somebody wants a lost warhammer back. Somebody else is renting a room, quiet tenants only.

A second board, smaller and less official: lost gear, room-for-rent scraps, one challenge to a duel that's clearly gone unanswered a long time. Anything worth chasing copies into your journal as a lead: a name and a place, nothing promised.
Still four silver. Still an insult.
He'll take it. Watch.
Board's behind you, same as it was a minute ago.
A crate shoved against the back wall, half-buried under someone else's forgotten kit.
Nothing there. Chalk dust and boot grit, and a floorboard worn pale where people wait to be called.
Nothing there. Somewhere behind the desk a drawer shuts. Guild business, and none of it yours.
Runner's Guild. Counter's open.

A teenage Drake, wiry, a strap-scarred satchel worn even behind the counter — she never fully sat down, she just stopped moving for a second. Slate-grey scales, a sweat-band she does not need indoors and wears anyway.
Couriers are made, not hired. Start with the market run. — the counter
THE DELIVERY BOARD. Your slip's still logged at the counter. Legs and ledgers don't care how it's going either.
THE DELIVERY BOARD. Legs and ledgers. Gold by distance, paid on the mark, same-waking terms. Slips at the counter.
...five more minutes.
A Gnoll runner, propped against the wall by the stool, legs out, boots still laced. Not asleep. Not far from it.
[Firefly] — The flame takes the birch on the second breath. Heat crawls out into the room and the stone begins giving it back.
A wide stone hearth, swept out and laid ready: split kindling under a lattice of dry birch, waiting on someone with a light. The mantel above it is worn smooth where wet gloves get slapped down.
Split kindling sits laid and ready under dry birch. The hearth is cold, and nobody here carries flint.
[Firefly] — The wick takes the flame and holds it. Yellow light spreads down the wall and over the slips pinned there.
[Light] — The orb slides into the lamp glass and settles. Yellow light spreads down the wall and over the slips pinned there.
A brass lamp bracketed to the wall over the slip rack, glass sooted at the top and dry as bone. The oil ran out some time ago and nobody has come back with more.
A wall lamp over the slip rack, glass sooted and wick dry. It has been dark long enough that the runners read by the door instead.
[Basic Cleaning] — You take it off in three passes. The dried mud lifts, the grain comes up pale, and the boards stop smelling of the road.
Road mud dried in ridges across the boards, stamped there by a week of packs set down hard. Somebody wiped one corner of it and gave up.
Dried road mud ridges the boards where pack after pack has come down on them. One corner is wiped clean and the rest is not.
Nothing there. Slip paper and rope wax. The whole room smells like somewhere else's mail.
Nothing there. Somebody's spare boots wait by the door, laces already loosened for the next run.
Yes, I am a [Necromancer]. No, I did not raise anything in this square. Move along, or ask me something worth my time.
A sniff - though a fractionally warmer one. You are... tolerable company. Rarer praise than you comprehend. I shall permit you to remain within conversational range.
Thin, immaculate, hungry in a way food will not fix. He holds himself like a duelist and watches hands, not faces. Whatever he studies, it is not small.
You set your shoulder to the grate. The rust gives with a shriek, and cold air breathes up out of the dark. Down you go.
Rust holds the bars, not a lock. The draft is steady — a tunnel, not a pit. The skittering keeps its distance. Something down there has learned to avoid shadows.
A heavy iron grate, rusted shut. Cold air rises from below, and something in the dark skitters away from your shadow.
Rust holds the bars, not a lock. The phial crate you eased down the rungs is gone from the ledge below. Collected, unbroken. Somewhere down there, someone's working glass got to keep being glass.
Busy, yes? Come back when you can talk.
You have a warm way about you, and warmth I can trade with. Come - for you, I will call it a fair price, and I will mean it. This is not nothing, from me.
A Gnoll with a merchant's smile and a soldier's eyes. She prices you the moment you approach, and remembers the number.
Too dark to see anything.
A plain door with dark behind it. The dust on the sill is scuffed one way. Something was dragged in, and not dragged out.
[Light] — The orb drifts down the stairs. There: Krshia's crate, dragged behind a broken shelf.
[Light] — The orb drifts down the stairs. Just an empty cellar now, and a scuff in the dust where the crate used to sit.
Pitch black past the first step. You'd need a light that travels with you.
A dray cart, a missing axle-pin, and a man about one shout from tipping the whole day over.
The sewer grates are backing up again and there's scavengers in the cellars. And paperwork. There's always the paperwork. Which is it?
Stripes on the sleeve, ink on the fingers. He would send the crate problem down the chain if the chain had not already sent it back up to him.
A worn marker stone, older than the buildings that grew up around it. Nobody living remembers who set it, or why it sits exactly here.
Cold, plain stone. Whatever it was for, it isn't for anything now.
Keep the gate clear. And if you're headed out, the road's got goblins on it lately. Watch knows. Watch is dealing with it.
The guard's mouth twitches toward a smile despite himself. Hah. You seem decent enough. Go on through easy - I'll remember the friendly one.
Watch armor, kept. He stands the post properly: weight even, eyes on the gap in the wall. Bored, but the boredom is a discipline, not a lapse.
The Worker pauses mid-errand and inclines its head. "This one is carrying goods for the market row. It is good work. Good day." It resumes, precisely.
An Antinium Worker — dark chitin, four arms, a crate balanced with unreasonable precision. It does not fidget. It does not need to.
The Worker stops sweeping. "This one was told the square must be clean. The square will be clean." It says it like a fact about tomorrow's weather.
Another Worker, identical to the first in the way coins from one mint are identical. It sweeps the same three cobbles until they answer for something.
The gate's my problem, so keep it dull and we'll get along fine.
Zevara's shoulders come down a fraction. Huh. Civil, and no bribe. You would not believe how short that list is. Go on through. And, thank you. Genuinely.

Oldblood Drake, light scales, a scar down the left of her jaw she's long past explaining. She reads the gate the way a clerk reads a ledger: every figure accounted for, and every one of them a suspect.
An Antinium of Liscor's Watch — dark chitin, four arms, antennae, twin swords worn at the hips like a closed argument. He stands still the way patient things do.
One moment; three columns into a tally. Say hello properly and I'll lose my place gladly.

Olesm brightens like a lamp. Oh! A friendly face. Most people's eyes glaze when I mention troop dispersal. Yours didn't. Would you... that is... care to see the board sometime? No pressure. A little pressure.

Thin, sky-blue scales, ink drying on three of his claws. A chess board waits at his elbow mid-game, played against himself, to feel how the other side thinks. His eyes are a wild, patterned blue, the one soft thing about a man who counts exits.
Loaves stacked in a pyramid that will not survive the lunch rush. A chalked board promises today's price, then a second, higher price scratched in for after the fourth bell.
Warm bread smell over the whole row. No one's minding the stall this exact moment. The loaves aren't going anywhere without a fight.
Watch gear, mostly honest.
A road-peddler behind a folding stall, half his stock still roped for travel. Everything he sells says somewhere else.
Silverfang goods laid out with a trap's care: cheapest at the front, the good stock where a browsing hand drifts. A note warns that the seller remembers faces.
Silverfang goods, honest prices. The Gnoll shopkeeper is off haggling somebody UP, elsewhere — she does not haggle down. A sign says she remembers faces, and debts.
