Silverfang goods, honest prices. The plains-wool bolt you carried up sits shelved at eye level, already half-sold by the yard. She moves what's good — and remembers who brought it.
Nothing there. A Drake shoulders past; Liscor has no patience for loiterers.
Nothing there. Gutter runoff and market noise two streets over, off a wall repointed twice.
Nothing there. Someone leans out an upstairs shutter, decides you are nothing, and pulls it to.
The shopfront door, hung so it swings shut on its own. Past it, the market tier goes back to being civic.
She pushes a bowl of salted something across the counter at you without being asked, and takes the coin for it without apologising.
A broad Drake behind a counter worn pale in two places, one where the coins land and one where her elbow goes. Both are hers.
Twelve forms about one crate. You get four pages in before the words stop meaning anything.
The shop's own copy of every form the crate has generated, in a stack tall enough to stand a cup on.

[Appraise Goods] — Form nine, clause four: perishable household stock is exempt from queue hold. Tin is not perishable. The salt packed WITH it is, and it is on the same manifest line. Four cycles, and the exemption was on the paper the whole time.
Forms, in an order. There is a shape to the order. You cannot see the shape.
A cleared square of floor by the back wall with a chalk outline on it, the size of one crate, waiting since the first cycle.
The dock is squared away for today. Whatever else moves, it moves tomorrow.
You square the load onto the chalk outline. It fits the way a thing fits when somebody measured it a month ago and has been looking at the empty space since.
Third leg, last leg. The crate lands inside its own chalk outline and something in the back of the shop goes quiet, then very loud, then quiet again.
Jars in a rank, labels in a hand that got neater partway along the shelf and then went back to how it was.
Half the jars are from tiers you will never have a permit for. The keeper does not explain how, and you decide not to ask in a city this fond of paperwork.
A bench cut down to knee height, three sets of claw-marks along the front edge at three different heights.
Something small goes very still behind the bench, decides you are not interesting, and resumes an argument you cannot follow about whose turn it is.
The family's own board: who eats here on credit, and for how long. Names in chalk, never in ink.
Eleven names carried. One of them has been carried for two years and has no repayment column at all. In Pallass, that is a document nobody filed.
Nothing there. Jars from tiers you will never hold a permit for, dusted anyway.
Nothing there. Something small breathes behind the bench and decides to keep still.
A workbench of calipers, weights, and chalk lines — every tool squared to the bench edge. The Magus is up at the office when he is not down here.
Every tool squared to the bench edge. You decide against touching anything.
Bar stock stacked by gauge, each bundle strapped and tagged. The tags carry a tier number, a bench number, and nothing else. No names anywhere on them.
Cold iron, cut to length by somebody who measured twice. The strapping doesn't give under your hand.
A standing barrel of water beside the anvil, skinned over with scale and grey all the way down. The rim is worn smooth in the two places a smith's hands go.
The water is warmer than the room around it. Something went in here not long ago.
Cooled slag and cracked crucible shards, heaped no higher than a line painted on the flagstones around it. The line has been repainted recently, and brightly.
Glassy black waste, still holding a little of the day's heat. Even the refuse up here has a level marked on it.

A bronze rail along the tier's open edge, polished bright by a hundred people leaning on the same stretch of it while they waited on the cage. Below it the shaft goes down past where the light gives up.
You put a hand on the rail. Warm from the tier, not from the drop. Whoever set it worked out exactly how close a person could stand.
A rack of numbered slips beside the second bench: a stock number, a bench number, an hour. No names on any of them. Any pair of hands that can read a gauge can take one down.
The rack is empty until the next shift files its slips. Pallass does not run two shifts at once.
You take a slip, walk its stock number down to the racks and the finished piece back up. The clerk who pays you writes down the hour you took, to the quarter.
The smith hands you the slip before the rack does. She says nothing about it. She wouldn't.
A wide iron-strapped door standing open on its wedge. Past it: a working hall, and a heat that has its own weather.
A civic bin beside the second bench, half full of work that never left the tier. Each piece has a tag, and every tag has the same examiner's seal on it.
Nine blades in the bin, all from one hand, all failed on the same measure. Somebody up here is doing careful work and failing it the same way every time.
A slate of what the cage is carrying today, chalked by hour. Two lines have been rewritten so many times the slate has gone smooth under them.
One crate of tin, den shop, market tier. Logged three cycles running and carried none of them. Beside it, in a tidier hand: HELD, QUEUE.
A pallet strapped and tagged and standing exactly where it has stood for three cycles, one hand's width outside the loading square.
The pallet is where you left it and the cage is where the bell says. Nothing moves again until the next shift.
You get the pallet onto the loading square and the strapping squared. The attendant looks at it, looks at the bell, and says nothing, which is the whole permission you are going to get.
An anvil bolted to its own slab, a furnace mouth banked low beside it — cold for now, but built to run hot for a working day at a time.
The metal underfoot still holds the day's heat, hours after the last hammer fell.
A second bench, same pattern as the first — built to the same civic spec as the market tier's stalls, just built for heat instead of trade.
Tool racks, empty for the moment. Whoever works this bench keeps it orderly.
A bronze grate exhales a slow white breath, steady as a held note. Somewhere below, something enormous is always working.
Warm, damp air. A rhythm underneath it, too even to be weather.
The brass gate rises with a well-oiled clank, counterweights turning smooth in their track. The lift carries you down, into the ordered quiet of the market tier.
The brass gate is locked. A stencilled plate: PERMIT AND STAMP REQUIRED. The clerk's window is open.
A bronze-riveted cage, tall enough to swallow a wagon, counterweights racked in a shaft that drops past sight. This is how the tiers actually connect.
A stone shape stands too near the tier's own edge, cracks along its arms glowing a shade too bright for the forge-heat alone.
She sets the hammer down long enough to look at you properly. From her, that reads as a whole conversation.
A Drake in a scarred leather apron, forearms banded with old burn-marks she stopped covering years ago. She works without looking up, and the work doesn't suffer for it.
He tips two fingers off the gate lever. "Quarter bell," he says, which from him is a kindness and a schedule at once.
A Drake in a brass-buttoned lift coat, one hand resting on the gate lever without gripping it. He watches the counterweights instead of the passengers, and knows where both are.
Tongs, swages and fullers hung in size order along a painted rack, every one of them chalk-outlined on the boards behind it. An empty outline is a tool somebody still has.
You lift a set of tongs off its outline and set it back. Heavier than it looks, and it goes back exactly straight.
Every bench on the tier chalked in a column, the smith's mark beside it and the hours they're owed. Two marks have been rubbed out and rewritten in a different hand.
Bench hours, to the quarter. Nobody up here works a minute they can't account for.
Nothing there. Warm metal underfoot, and a rhythm below it that never quite stops.
Nothing there. Every tool on this tier is squared to an edge somebody measured.
The hall door, propped with a wedge nobody has ever removed. Past it, the tier's noise resumes.
Heat, metal, and a gauge you cannot read. Guessing here costs somebody a week.
A billet clamped mid-process, the quench beside it, a gauge nobody has reset since the last failure. Somebody stopped here on purpose and did not come back.
[Appraise Goods] — You read the grain off the colour, hold the count two beats longer than the slate says, and quench. The billet comes out with the standard's own answer in it.
Colour, count, quench. You can see there is an order to it. You cannot see the order.
A civic notice pinned at eye height, examiner's seal at the corner, the text underneath it read so often the ink has gone grey where thumbs land.
The standard does not measure how hard a blade comes out. It measures how it RECOVERS. Somebody up here has been failing the wrong test perfectly.
She looks up for exactly as long as the count allows, then back down. From an apprentice on the clock, that is a warm welcome.
A young Drake with her sleeves pinned back and a scorch on one forearm she has not stopped working long enough to notice.
Water gone grey with scale, a skin of oil across the top, and a scum line three fingers above the current level.
You touch the surface. Warm all the way down. This tub has not been cold in years, and the scum line says nobody has ever had time to change it.
A slate ruled into columns: heat, count, quench, result. The result column is chalked over so many times the surface has gone soft.
Forty-one attempts. Under the last one, in smaller writing than the rest: TRY THE OTHER WAY ROUND.
Finished pieces racked in a grid, each with a civic tag wired to it. They are not for sale. They are the argument.
Every piece on the wall passed. You count the tags: four different smiths, four different answers, one standard. Pallass framed the disagreement and hung it up.
The rig swings past its own marks and settles wrong, again and again. Whatever is out of true in it is the forge's business — until somebody on this floor makes it yours.
A squat rig on three legs, gauges banked along its front, correcting its own posture a half-beat after it needs to.
Nothing there. Quench water and hammer scale, under a wall of work that all passed.
Nothing there. The heat in here keeps a schedule, and you are not on it.

A squared plinth of the same slab the whole tier is cut from. No rune, no seam, nothing carved into it at all — and still the blankness has an outline, the way a mould does. Whatever door reaches this tier is already remembered here.
Cold, precise stone, and not as blank as it looks. Something the shape of a door is being held in it, patiently, for later.
State your business and your sponsor, or stand aside for the next in line.
Measure twice. I have measured everything in this hall at least three times, and I am still finding what I missed.
The brass gate rises with a well-oiled clank, counterweights turning smooth in their track. The lift carries you up, into noise and heat and orange light.
The brass gate is locked. A stencilled plate: PERMIT AND STAMP REQUIRED. The clerk's window is open.
A bronze-riveted cage, tall enough to swallow a wagon, counterweights racked in a shaft that drops past sight. This is how the tiers actually connect.
The rail, the drop, the haze. Pallass keeps its details above your pay grade.
[Eagle Eyes] — The haze gives up. Nine tiers resolve into stalls, patrol routes, and one dropped coin purse on a ledge two floors down that everyone else is too proud to see.
No more dropped coins by the railing today. Pallass sweeps on schedule.
Nine tiers of city below, if your eyes are good enough to spend on it.
Two grey shapes stand either side of an unclaimed stall, carved plating catching the tier's flat light, neither one moving.
Cunning Crafts! Best components on the tier, or the second-best, depending who is asking and how much they are buying.
A City Gnoll in a stained apron, shaggy fur tan under the stains, eyebrows singed down to stubble. He is arguing cheerfully with himself about the price of something.
You look like someone who could use a potion. Everyone can use a potion. Mine are only occasionally on fire — once.
A young human woman behind a fold-out consignment stall, talking fast, pricing three things at once and watching your hands to see which one you will pick up.
A working alchemist's bench, burners cold. You would not know where to start.
Cheap reagents racked by the burner, and a scorch-ring on the slate where a hundred crude workings went slightly wrong.
[Low-Grade Synthesis] — Crude reagents over a low flame, and a draught that mostly does what it should. It will pass.
Xif's spare bench, scrubbed and stocked. A low flame and a steady hand would turn it into something.
A glass drip-still, coiled and cold. The magic-water in it means nothing to you yet.
A coil of glass tubing over a low pan, magic-water beading down it one clarified drop at a time.
[Magic-Water Solvent] — The magic-water comes off the coil clear enough to bend the light. One phial, corked and ready.
A drip-still set for magic-water. Someone who knows the working could draw a clean solvent from it.
A bulb of dark glass over cold coals, half full of something grey. Not your trade.
A distilling retort, its bulb crusted white at the neck where the salts climb as the wash boils away.
[Mineral Distillation] — You boil the wash honest and slow. What is left is a spoonful of pale salts, the backbone of the next working.
A retort over a banked fire, a mineral wash already loaded. A distiller could boil it down to salts.
State your business and your sponsor. Everyone's business goes through this window eventually.
The good bench wants both halves of the working in hand: a solvent phial and a measure of mineral salts. You are short at least one.
The best bench Xif owns, kept for work you cannot do yet.
The bench Xif keeps for himself: clean glass, a steady blue burner, and room laid out for two reagents to become a third.
[True Synthesis] — Solvent into salts, in the one order that holds. What settles in the vial is clearer than either half went in.
The finest bench on the tier, and it knows it. A true synthesis needs solvent and salts both, and a hand that can bring them together.
The still wants a crude draught to work down. Your pack has nothing worth reducing.
A reduction still, hissing faintly. The valves mean nothing to you.
A copper still on a slow flame, built to boil a crude draught down to what it should have been the first time.
[Perfect Reduction] — The still takes the crude draught apart and returns only the part that matters, clear as morning.
Xif's reduction still, all coils and patience. In the right hands it turns crude work into clean.

Civic ordinances under glass, numbered and dated, the oldest one on the wall older than the wall. Nothing is pinned over anything else. There is a numbered slot for every notice and no notice without a slot.
Ordinances, numbered and glassed. Somewhere in Pallass a clerk owns the key to this case, and only that clerk.
Ordinance 44, third column: tier passes are the property of the city and the responsibility of the bearer. Yours is in your pocket, and now you know whose it is.

A weighing pillar set out where anyone can use it, brass pans hanging true, the city's own test weights chained to the column. Any stallkeeper's measure can be checked here against the city's, in front of everyone.
You set a hand on the pan and it swings back level. The chained weights have inspection dates stamped into them, the last one this month.
A shopfront wedged between two civic frontages, the only door on this row with a hand-painted sign and something cooking behind it.
A rank of low carts for hire, each chalked with a tier number and a rate, and a queue board nobody is standing at.
The rank is empty until the next rotation. Pallass hires carts on a schedule too.
You take a cart off the rank, walk the crate off the lift apron and across two blocks of very orderly stone, and nobody stops you once. The paperwork was never about the crate.
Second leg, same cart, same two blocks. The rank clerk marks it without looking up, which in Pallass is a commendation.
Empty crates stacked a head above the awnings behind the stalls. The razorbeak has decided they belong to the razorbeak, and no stallkeeper has argued yet.

It goes up off the crates and comes back screaming about the west end. The two standing things down there step aside for anyone whose permit is already filed — and the office that files it is the counter four stalls behind you.
Rows of chalked figures, precise to the copper, refreshed each morning by a clerk with steadier hands than yours. Nobody haggles here. Nobody needs to.
Chalk and slate. The numbers don't move for anyone.
A stall built to the same civic pattern as every other on this tier — same counter height, same awning pitch, same posted-price placard. Efficient. Impersonal.
Goods arranged in neat rows, prices chalked and unmoving. The stallkeeper barely looks up — the price is the price.
A stall built to the same civic pattern as every other on this tier — same counter height, same awning pitch, same posted-price placard. Efficient. Impersonal.
Goods arranged in neat rows, prices chalked and unmoving. The stallkeeper barely looks up — the price is the price.
A stall burner, hot and jealously watched. Renting it takes more than coin — it takes credentials.
[Advanced Cooking] — You cook on a stranger's fire in a city of critics, and the critics go quiet.
The stallkeeper's burner is free between rushes. Pallass argues about everything except good food.
A stall built to the same civic pattern as every other on this tier — same counter height, same awning pitch, same posted-price placard. Efficient. Impersonal.
Goods arranged in neat rows, prices chalked and unmoving. The stallkeeper barely looks up — the price is the price.
The price is on the board. It'll be the same price however long you stare at it.
A bronze grate exhales a slow white breath, steady as a held note. Somewhere below, something enormous is always working.
Warm, damp air. A rhythm underneath it, too even to be weather.
The window ledge is worn smooth where a thousand wrists have rested, waiting on a stamp. A stencilled plate lists the posted fees. Nobody argues with it.
Forms, inkwells, and a bell that has clearly been rung far too many times.
Nothing there. Chalked prices and swept stone, and not one thing outside its allotted square.
Nothing there. A clerk two stalls down writes something about you and moves on.
A straw-tick pallet against the wall, blanket already turned down for whoever needs it.
Straw tick, borrowed blanket — Riverfarm always finds room for one more.
A ledger left open on the corner table, the same one he carries everywhere else. Columns re-summed in three different inks — he never trusts the first count, or the second.
Grain against debts, and the debts keep winning most years. Best not to read it over his shoulder.
A thin man with a hazel stick in each hand, laying them side by side against the light.
Sacks stacked low and a season coming for them. Lifting them above the flood line is work, and work is a Skill you either have or you don't.
Grain sacks stacked at ankle height on a shed floor, with the river three weeks out.
[Basic Cleaning] — You clear the shed floor and stack every sack up off the boards. The count comes right the moment anyone can see all of it at once.
[Basic Cooking] — You feed the flood crew out of the mill's own pot, and they work the shed twice over for it. The count comes right in the doing.
Something has been at the sacks in that corner. Nobody here has called it a problem yet, and it is not your count to go digging in.
Chaff scattered wide, sacks opened low down, and something breathing behind the last row.
A ladder down into a pit of black water, with the wheel standing still in it and the sluice pinned shut against the season.
The pinned sluice carries three seasons of high-water scratches, and each one sits higher than the last.
A shelf set higher on the wall than any shelf needs to be, with notches and years cut into the post beside it.
Somebody has cut a notch for every flood since before the village had a headman, and built the shelf a hand above the worst of them.
A bundle of split hazel sticks hung on a nail, each notched down one edge.
Split tallies. One half stays with the mill, one half goes home with the household, and neither can be altered alone.
Fresh-turned earth, packed and raised into a long low wall. Someone's been digging with purpose, not just drainage.
Just raised earth. Whatever it's for, nobody's finished it yet.
Low fence rail, bordering the tilled rows.
Low fence rail, bordering the tilled rows.
Low fence rail, bordering the tilled rows.
Rails re-set forty paces east of where they stood. The gap they left is the corusdeer road, and the hoof marks say the herd found it.
Rails re-set forty paces east of where they stood. The gap they left is the corusdeer road, and the hoof marks say the herd found it.
Low fence rail, bordering the tilled rows.
Low fence rail, bordering the tilled rows.
Low fence rail, bordering the tilled rows.
Not now. Got a village to hold together.
A ledger under one arm, mud to the knee, the look of a man doing three jobs badly instead of one job well.
Ordinary, except for how still they stand, and a faint red thread at the wrist that doesn't match anything else they're wearing.
One long thatch ridge, twice the width of any cottage. Smoke curls from a vent at the peak even in daylight.
Hollow's not safe alone.
Rope-burned hands, a game bag, and wolf sign on his boots. Whatever he hunts, it walks on four legs.

A worn marker stone at the village's heart. Someone scratched a spiral into its face, long since softened by weather. Attunement is what markers like this are cut for: a door shown the right stone learns the place, and can open onto it ever after.
Cold, plain stone, and it stays cold for you. Whatever hung a door somewhere else hasn't hung one yet.
A narrow break in the treeline, west of the fields. The light changes past the first few trees.
Nothing there. Whatever you saw is gone with the light.
Eyes catch the light at the field's edge, gone again when you look straight at them. Only after dark.
Vines thicker than they should be, over the fence line and into the village since the thicket business settled. They creep across open ground, twitching against a wind that isn't blowing.
A plank of hooks at the fence line, each hook holding a scrap with a task on it and no name. Ditching, thatch, a fence a cow disagrees with. The scraps come down about as fast as they go up.
Every hook is bare. Riverfarm doesn't invent work to keep a stranger busy.
You take a scrap off its hook and spend the morning behind it. Ditching, mostly. The village pays coin because coin is the thing it has least of, and it pays on the day.
Somebody chalked your name against a hook before you got there. That is the whole of Riverfarm's vocabulary for gratitude, and it is not a small word.
The hook you get is the one nobody else will touch: the wet corner down by the river, every time. They give it to you because you finish it.
The mill's ground-floor door, set into the base of the tower on the river side. The sluice hums even with the wheel pinned.
Hurdle fencing the hunter threw up after the thicket business. Two ewe lambs inside it, and a third that will not put weight on a foreleg.
[Beast's Mending] — You strap the lamb's leg, and it stands on it before you have finished. The ewes crowd in to look.
The lambs have had their handling for today. Crowd them now and you undo it.
You get a hand under the limping one and hold it until it stops shaking. Fleece comes away on your fingers.
They come to the rail for you now. You work burrs out of three fleeces and leave the bad leg for last.
A scatter of old bones in the field grass, half sunk. The wolf keeps returning to it, head down, digging and stopping and digging again.
Under a stone, under the turf: a thin copper ring, polished bright by somebody's worried thumbs before they lost it here.
Turned earth, filled in and gone quiet. The wolf walks past it now.
The stringers are sound and the boards are somewhere downriver. Standing here wishing at it will not deck it.
Two stringers still run out along the bank from the cottage corner, and the decking between them is gone — lifted by a flood and never replaced. The beams are sound. It is boards it wants.
[Basic Repair] — You cut and lay boards across the stringers until the walk is a walk again. It holds when you lean on it, and it will hold tomorrow.
Clay-daub walls, a low thatch roof. A washing line strung between two posts.
Someone's home. Best not to just walk in.
The bank is cut clean through here, down to brown water. You could go the long way round the cottage, or somebody could put boards back across it.
Where the decking used to be there is a scoured trench down to the water, wider than a stride and undercut on both lips.
You get one sack up and your back tells you about the other eleven. This is a job for somebody built for it.
Grain sacks stacked off a dray at the bank head, waiting on however many trips it takes. Two men are looking at them the way you look at a long afternoon.
[Broader Shoulders] — You take three at once and walk them up to the shed without stopping. The dray is clear before the second man has picked up his first, and two coins come your way for it.
The dray is empty and the shed is full. Nothing more to shift today.
Dragging them one at a time will take all day. Carrying them properly would not.
A second cottage, smaller, its thatch newer than its neighbor's.
Someone's home. Best not to just walk in.
Sails turning slow in whatever wind there is. The grinding floor above the wheat fields.
The sails creak overhead. No one's tending it right now.
A stone-ringed well, rope worn smooth by years of hauling. The water's clean this far from the blight talk.
Cool water, a long way down. You leave the rope where you found it.
Bundled and stacked before the rain, the way a good harvest gets stored.
Straw and an old coat, arms out over the tilled rows. It isn't working today — there are crows on its own hat.
A plank pier reaching out over the river. The village's whole trade with anywhere downstream starts here (wiki Riverfarm, ch. 3.00-3.01 E: 'farming land fed by a river').
Weathered planks, sound underfoot. The current runs steady past the end of it.
Low fence rail, bordering the tilled rows.
A tree grown crooked, leaning in over the path like it's listening.
A stone taller than it should be able to stand on its own, glowing faint purple at the seams.
Another of the ring-stones, humming faintly if you hold still.
Another of the ring-stones, humming faintly if you hold still.
Something's meant to go in this, cooked properly. You don't know your way around a stew pot. Yet.
An iron pot set by the cottage door, empty and waiting. Someone means for it to be used.
[Basic Cooking] — You cook the offering plain and honest, the way you'd feed anyone who'd walked far to eat.
The pot waits for something cooked plain and honest.
The kettle wants yarrow before it gives anything back.
A witch's cauldron, warm and waiting. Whatever it wants from you, it isn't just stirring.
[Hedge Remedy] — You stir like you're sorry for the sick, the way she said. What comes off the ladle is the color of meaning it.
The cauldron's lit and the water's talking to itself. Hands that mean it could bring a remedy out of that.
A row of cold candle-stubs, set either side of the door. Whatever lights them, it isn't a match.
Cold wax and old wicks, set along the threshold like they're waiting for something specific.
[Light] — The candles catch, one after another, without a flame ever touching them.
Cold candle-stubs either side of the door. No match will do it.
Roots and briar, knotted tighter than any plant ties itself. Whatever it's holding, an untrained eye won't find it.
A snarl of root and briar at the center of the standing stones, tied in a knot that doesn't look like it grew that way.

[Observe] — The knot isn't wood at all, once you look right at it: a price, tied off and waiting to be paid. You pay it yourself, plainly, and the tension goes out of the air like a held breath let go.
The knot is too deliberate for briar. It wants a closer look than eyes give for free.
A standing stone, older than the village and not saying anything about it.
[Detect Magic] — Light runs under the turf in one long seam, straight through the stone and away west. The hollow is built on a current.
The stone sits where the ground feels heaviest. That's not an accident.
Tea's still hot. The offer doesn't get warmer with asking twice.
A small grey witch in a hat pressed with tea leaves and old flowers. She holds a cup like the answer to a question you haven't asked yet.
Briars, moving without wind. They haven't noticed you yet.
A tree grown crooked, leaning in over the path like it's listening.
More briars, thicker here, coiled tight around something you can't quite see.
The trees thin out this way. Open fields past the last few trunks.
The brambles here twist into a tight loop, low to the ground. It doesn't look natural. You can't tell how to clear it without setting it off.
You work the knot loose one bramble at a time, careful of the thorns. Snagged in the weave: a coin, tarnished green from the damp.
The briar holds nothing new today.
Brambles knotted into a tight loop, low against the undergrowth. Nothing grows that way on its own.
A second, smaller house at the hollow's west edge, its roof half fallen in. The lintel is cut with a line of shallow marks, worn nearly smooth, and the door stands open on the dark.
The bracken is pressed flat and the smell of it is old. Nothing about this is your business until somebody tells you otherwise.
Bracken pressed flat in a hollow under the northern trees, and the smell of something that has been eating well.
A tree grown crooked, leaning in over the path like it's listening.
A tree grown crooked, leaning in over the path like it's listening.
A tree grown crooked, leaning in over the path like it's listening.
A tree grown crooked, leaning in over the path like it's listening.
A tree grown crooked, leaning in over the path like it's listening.
A tree grown crooked, leaning in over the path like it's listening.
A tree grown crooked, leaning in over the path like it's listening.
A mossy, sagging roof, a crooked chimney, and one window that's always lit no matter the hour.
The door's shut. Whatever's inside isn't asking for company right now.
A palm-sized shard of grey stone on the shelf, cut along one edge with marks you cannot read.
A shard of grey stone on the shelf, set down carefully by someone who meant to come back for it.

[Detect Magic] — The shard is one link of a boundary that used to ring the whole thicket. It still pulls, faintly, along the exact line the deer refuse to cross. It was drawn to keep something in, and it has been failing at that for a very long time.
The scrap hums under the dust, and not the way dust hums.
A row of stoppered jars along the top shelf, their labels faded to a suggestion.
Every stopper is waxed and every jar is still full. Whoever kept this house left it ready and never came back for it.
A rack of bundled stems, dried long past any use.
Yarrow, mostly, and a great deal of it. Somebody kept this place stocked for a house they intended to come back to.
Cold ash banked neatly against the back of the hearth.
The ash is banked the way you bank a fire you mean to wake in the morning. It has been cold for years.
One shutter, latched, with daylight coming through the slats in bars.
Latched from the inside, and the hut was shut when you found it. You decide not to work that through any further today.

East past the gate road, across the floodplains — this is the ruin. Survey stakes, a banked fire, and someone's washing on a line: the Horns got here first. The sealed level is deeper in, under the pedestal court.
The near plate's twin, set apart in the rubble, spiral running the other way. Cold, until its partner isn't.
Cold stone, unlit. The spiral wants something the press alone doesn't give.
Both spirals light — red, then a clean white. The pedestal's seam exhales dust.
"Good," she says, once, and goes back to the rope. From Yvlon that lands about like a hand on the shoulder.
Armour half off and stacked in the order it goes back on. She has braced the gap's lip with two stakes and a plank, and she tests the plank every time she passes it.
"You are a known quantity now," Ksmvr says. "That is the highest category I have."
Three coils of rope laid out in exact parallel, and an Antinium re-counting them, because the count is the point and the rope is only the rope.
A board of pinned sheets under a scrap of tarp: a plan of the court, a rope tally, and a list of four names with hours beside them. The hours are shared out even.
Ceria's hand, mostly. The court plan is drawn twice, and the second drawing corrects the first without comment.
Spoil from the gap, sorted into two heaps: worked stone in one, plain rubble in the other. Somebody is keeping every piece a chisel ever touched.
Broken stone, sorted by whether anyone shaped it. The carved heap is the smaller one and by a long way the tidier.
Three lengths of rope, whipped at the ends and hung off a driven stake so that none of it lies in the wet.
Good rope, dry, coiled by somebody who has watched bad rope let go.
Stakes driven at intervals nobody eyeballed, string run between them, chalk numbers on every one. The line stops dead at the mouth of the pedestal court and does not go in.
The string is taut. Somebody re-tensions it each morning, which is not a thing four adventurers usually bother to do.
Ringed stones around a scatter of white ash, and four flattened squares of ground where bedrolls were. The stakes have been pulled and stacked, the string wound back onto its spool.
Cold days ago. They struck the camp properly, filled the pit, and took the rope with them. Whatever the Horns came down here for, they carried it home.
Banked low and fed on whatever burns down here. Somebody turns it every few hours; the ash is raked, not spilled.
A cookfire kept small on purpose, ringed with stones somebody carried in. It has been burning longer than a day.
Rope, spare stakes, a folded tarp, and three days of dried rations for four people. Packed by someone who has done this before.
The expedition's supply crate, lid roped shut against the damp.
Mind the survey stakes. We put them there for a reason.
A faceless stone sentinel leans over the court, its shield worn smooth by grit and years. The stance still points toward the cracked plinth.
The sentinel's face is gone, but its posture survives: shield toward the court, warning anyone who follows its gaze.
A stone rests in a shallow cradle atop the plinth, held there by nothing you can see. Something older than the dust stands close enough to notice you noticing.

Below the pedestal: not treasure. A DOOR — unhung, unmarked, utterly ordinary except that four adventurers go silent around it at once. Ceria, finally: 'That's wardwork. Old, fed wardwork. We're taking it home.' The anchor stone comes up with it.
Beneath where the door lay, still seated in its groove: the anchor stone. The Horns left nothing else behind.
The stone doesn't move. Whatever holds it there is still standing guard, close enough that reaching for it feels like a very bad idea.
The seal is broken, but the warding still holds the stone fast. Two spiral plates flank the court — the carving beside the pedestal looks like a beginning.

The seal is broken and the Horns are already down the gap — Yvlon bracing, Ksmvr counting rope. The warding still holds the stone fast. Two spiral plates flank the court; Ceria points at the carving beside the pedestal and says that one's a beginning.

Both spirals hold their light, and the seam under the plinth stops fighting your hand. Whatever the ward was keeping out, it was never the plates — it was whoever hadn't walked them. Ceria, already reaching for rope: 'Ksmvr. Down. Carefully.'
The cradle on top is empty and the seam beneath it stands open on nothing. Whatever the ruin was built around, the ruin isn't holding it any more.
A carved socket in the ruin stone. Whatever sat here, someone carried it off.
[Detect Magic] — The socket still remembers its stone: a slow pulse, counting toward a door that already left. The warding reads near-first: the spiral beside the pedestal, then its far twin.

[Detect Magic] — You read the binding the way Pisces reads a page, and the reading is the undoing: the ward was keyed to whatever stood guard here, and a keyed ward answers anyone who can say the key back. The seal lets go. Ceria, from the gap: 'Do that again and I'm putting you on the ledger.'
The socket's empty, but empty like a held breath. The warding reads near-first — the spiral beside the pedestal, then its far twin.
Stone shaped like a soldier, or close enough that the difference doesn't help you. It hasn't moved since you stepped into this room. That is not the same as harmless.

The stone soldier still stands, and the cradle it stands over is empty. Whatever it was set here to keep was carried out past it and it did not move. A ward outlasts the thing it warded. That is the whole nature of a ward.
The bones rise and fall into step behind you.
Old bones, settled where they fell. They are not going anywhere. Probably.
A palm-sized plate set flush beside the pedestal, cut with a spiral that walks inward. Faint warmth, like a banked coal.
The spiral takes the press and holds a dull red glow. Something in the pedestal shifts its weight.

A ring of fire-blackened stones, the ash inside long dead and cold. Something sat here in the dark and knew how to keep a fire — or learned how, the way they say these things learn, when the moon is full and their minds come clear.
A fire-pit ringed with blackened stones, its ashes cold. Whoever tended it had hands enough to strike a spark, and left gnawed bones banked around the edge, cracked for their marrow.

A midden of cracked bones, marrow sucked clean. Gnoll, most of them. A few too large to name. They have been sorted, almost stacked, as though something down here counts its meals and keeps the score.
A heap of gnawed bones, splintered for their marrow. Some are Gnoll. One is a Drake's. They are stacked, not scattered. And that is worse than if they had been.
The bones rise and fall into step behind you.
Old bones, settled where they fell. They are not going anywhere. Probably.

Two of them crouch where the tunnel narrows, moon-grey and mountain-shouldered, knuckles to the stone. Their small eyes track you without blinking. Between you and the deeper dark, they are the door — and the lock.
The gallery floor slopes down past where the den used to be, into a chamber someone else has clearly been surveying.

The passage opens into a vast pillared gallery, its floor packed smooth by generations of pacing feet. Eyes catch your light far back in the dark and slide away. This is where they den, and where the big one waits, breathing slow in the black.
The tunnel widens into a pillared gallery, the air stirring with breath that is not your own. Something large shifts in the dark ahead, and the pacing scuffs go quiet. You have found the warren.
The gallery is silent now. The pacing tracks are old and dust-softened; nothing breathes in the dark ahead. Past the emptied den, the stone the Watch sealed stands unbroken.
Claw-gouges score the pillars, going quiet toward the back. The den is empty — cleared, then sealed. Whatever the warren was, it is a grave and a door now.
There it is. Big one first. Questions after.

It fills the gallery mouth like a landslide that learned to breathe: upright, moon-grey, a pale mane over shoulders wider than a doorway. Old scars cross its hide, and a Gnoll's picked bones lie stacked at its feet. Its eyes hold on you with something worse than hunger: thought.
Sinew and bone hooks, strung low across the gallery floor. It has the shape of something meant to catch. You don't know how to spring it safely.
You work the hooks free of the sinew line and let it fall slack. Wedged in the rig: a couple of coins, old and green with tarnish.
You've picked this snare clean today. The warren restocks on its own schedule.
Sinew and bone hooks, strung low across the gallery floor. Whatever set it hunts down here, same as you.
A single page, gone soft with damp, wedged where the old brick has cracked.
I'm fine. Really. Just — turned around in the dark, that's all.
A length of wire runs low across the passage, pinned to a rusted stanchion. Whatever it's meant to catch, you can't tell how to spring it safe.
You ease the wire off its catch and coil it loose. A few scavenged links clatter free, worth a coin or two melted down.
Nothing else glints in the nest today.
Wire, taut and low, strung off a rusted stanchion. Something in the nest rigged this. Careful hands could clear it.
Bone and wire, tangled at the drain mouth. It has the shape of a trap. You can't read it well enough to touch it — that's trap-craft, a rogue's trade.
You work the bone pins loose and unwind the wire. A few coins sit wedged in the silt beneath it, dropped by whoever it once caught.
The drain has given up all it's going to give today.
Bone and wire, tangled at the drain mouth, rigged for something bigger than rats. A steady hand could clear it.
A little iron strongbox, silt-caked, dragged here by someone who never came back for it.
The hinge shears off in your hand. Inside: a wax-wrapped roll of coin, dry as the day it was hidden. 6 gold.
[Firefly] — Fire catches the tarred rope and runs greedily through the pile. In moments it is ash, the nook stands open, and the pale glint turns out to be a strongbox handle.
Sodden timber and tarred rope, jammed wall to wall. You could haul at it for an hour, or you could burn it, if you had the means to make fire.

A slumped heap of waterlogged timber and old rope, tarred black and long dead. It chokes the little side-nook past the ladder — and something pale glints between the boards, too deep to reach. Dry enough on top to take a flame, if you had one.
Pale green moss crusts the old brick in patches, breathing a cold light that never quite reaches the water. Drakes farmed it once, they say, to see down here without lanterns.
Phosphor moss clings to the brick, glowing a sick, cold green. Cool to the touch, and it hisses faintly when your shadow crosses it.
A carved stone boundary marker, Drake glyphs worn shallow. It counts cisterns and sluice-gates in a hand two centuries dead. Someone scratched a newer mark beside it: a spider, hastily.
An old Drake drainage marker, its glyphs half-swallowed by grime. You can just make out a map of channels — and a fresh scratch, shaped like a spider, gouged over the third cistern.
A market crate, swollen and burst, washed down through a grate above. Whatever was in it fed something down here long ago.
A ruined crate, half-sunk in silt. Merchant stamps still show under the rot: lost cargo, swallowed by the sewers and picked clean.
Cable-thick silk, black-and-silver banded, stretched wall to wall. Not a house spider's work. Something with a shield on its back spun this, and recently.
Ropes of banded silk choke the side passage, strong as wire. Wrapped in it, drained pale: a rat, a boot, something that used to be a Watchman's lantern.

Two of them, banded carapaces catching the moss-light, waiting where the silk is thickest. Their legs test the air toward you. Behind them the tunnel drops away, and more eyes catch the light down there than you want to count.
The ledge overlooks the nest: a perfect vantage, if you had the eye to read one. You don't, quite. Not yet.

[Appraise Foe] — You lie flat on the ledge and read the nest like a map. Two sentries on the silk, a brood-hollow behind them, and a tunnel dropping away toward the Dungeon proper. That's where the rest of them are. Count, size, exits: you have it all, and you never had to draw a blade.
A perfect vantage over the nest, for a trained eye.
You lower yourself into the fissure. The sewer's damp falls away behind you, and a dry, ancient cold rises to meet your hands. The dark below swallows the last of the light from above.

The floor gave way here, not long ago: a raw crack breathing air colder and older than the sewers ever hold. The claw-scores on its lip all point one way: down. Something climbed up through this, and means to again.
A fresh fissure splits the sewer floor, exhaling a dry, breathing cold from far below. Deep gouges rake the stone lip. Something big has been using this as a door.
